title: Modal divisions, temporal possibility, modal propositions, and why modality is considerational
en:
... or is considered a **copula**. For example, in *a human is a writer*, existence may be left wholly unspoken; yet we cannot plausibly say that the proposition does not mean either *he exists as a writer* or *writing is established for him*, but means only that whatever one concept applies to the other does also. The investigators find no substantive difference between *is established for*, *exists for*, *is truly predicated of*, or *is borne as a predicate by*: these differ only verbally. What we have argued accords with the *Tajrīd*.

**Possibility is intrinsic only.** Were it extrinsic, the thing would be, in itself, either necessary or impossible—necessarily existent or nonexistent—and subsequently through something else become such that neither existence nor nonexistence was necessary. An intrinsic character would then be eliminated by something other than it, a manifest impossibility. This is what is meant by a modal **reversal** (*inqilāb*).

**On the several senses of possibility.** *Special possibility* (*imkān khāṣṣ*) negates the necessity both of existence and of nonexistence and is opposed to intrinsic necessity and impossibility alike. If *possible* negates only necessity of existence, it opposes necessity and extends to the specially possible and the intrinsically impossible: even an impossible thing can be said to have **possible nonexistence**. If it negates necessity of nonexistence, it opposes impossibility and extends both to specially possible things and to necessary beings, so the Necessary has **possible existence** in that broad sense. This is close to ordinary language and is therefore called **general or common possibility** (*imkān ʿāmm*): people hear *possible to exist* as *not impossible to exist*, and *possible not to exist* as *not impossible not to exist*.

Some mistakenly suppose that general possibility is a **single concept** comprehending the necessary, impossible, and specially possible alike by negating the necessity of **either one** of the two sides, existence or nonexistence. But when we call something possible without qualification, that is not what is ordinarily understood; possibility **of existence** denies impossibility, while possibility **of nonexistence** denies necessity. The broad possible is therefore contrasted with the impossible and includes the necessary, as when a universal is classified into the impossible and the possible, one subdivision of the possible being a concept of which exactly one individual can exist and all others are excluded—the Necessary Existent. This also disposes of a puzzle about the logical rule that the negation of a more general predicate is narrower than the negation of a more specific one. One cannot infer that whatever is **not generally possible** is nevertheless **specially possible**, by confusing the two different scopes of the expression *possible*: the seeming paradox relies on a spurious single general possibility common to both opposite modalities.

**Future possibility.** Sometimes *possible* is taken with respect exclusively to a future event, without considering past or present. Possibility is opposed to necessity, and a thing appears the more possible the less it is subject to some necessity. What has happened or is happening has already been determined as occurring or not occurring, whereas the future is not yet known to have one of those statuses. Some therefore require the thing to be **nonexistent now** for its future existence to be possible, since present existence is already a necessity. **Objection:** present nonexistence also constitutes a present necessity; if both are to be excluded, the subject must now be neither existent nor nonexistent, denying both contradictories or requiring them both. **Clarification:** those who require present nonexistence likely mean the possibility **that existence newly supervene** in the future. That requires that its **occurrence now be absent**, not the possibility that nonexistence itself first occur. Conversely, future possibility **that nonexistence newly supervene**, that is, future cessation, presupposes present existence. No contradiction is involved once the object of the possibility is specified.

**Dispositional possibility** (*imkān istiʿdādī*) is the readiness of matter to receive forms and accidents after certain causes and conditions are in place but before their total cause is complete and the effect is necessary. It admits degrees of proximity and remoteness according to how many requisite conditions are present, as humanity is progressively prepared in semen, embryo stages, and later development, or writing becomes more readily attainable for a fetus, child, and finally a pupil who learns. Unlike intrinsic possibility, this readiness is not an inseparable concomitant of quiddity: it begins with conditions that previously were lacking and ceases when the prepared object is actually realized.

**The attachment of possibility.** Quiddity taken together with its existence, or the existence of its cause, is **necessary through another**. Taken with its nonexistence, or the absence of its cause, it is **impossible through another**. It is only when considered neither with those actual conditions nor with their negations—but as itself, and related in thought to existence—that pure intrinsic **possibility** is conceived. Thus possibility can be separated from extrinsic necessity and impossibility **in conception**: do not take account of either the quiddity's or its cause's existence or nonexistence. It cannot ordinarily be separated from them in external reality, since every possible entity either exists, and so is necessitated through another, or does not exist, and so is impossible through another, unless one endorses the intermediate state between existence and nonexistence.

**Relations among necessity and impossibility through another.** Both are called *necessity* or *necessitation*, the first of **existence** and the second of **nonexistence**. If the adjunct is reversed—necessity of existence alongside impossibility of nonexistence—they are coextensive: whatever must exist through another cannot fail to exist through another, and conversely; likewise whatever must not exist through another cannot exist through another. If both qualifications concern the **same** side, existence or nonexistence, they exclude each other: nothing can both be necessarily existent and impossibly existent. These two extrinsic modalities are **mutually exclusive but not exhaustive**, since neither applies to the intrinsically necessary or intrinsically impossible. They may, however, **exchange** in a possible thing: an effect that was necessarily existent through its cause can cease when the cause ceases, and then its existence becomes impossible through another; a formerly absent possible effect becomes necessary through another once its cause is realized.

Intrinsic necessity and intrinsic impossibility are likewise mutually exclusive but not exhaustive, since neither applies to intrinsically possible things, and **neither can convert into the other**. Intrinsic and extrinsic **necessity** are also mutually exclusive but not exhaustive, as are intrinsic and extrinsic **impossibility**. The extrinsically necessary or impossible is intrinsically possible, unlike the intrinsically necessary or impossible; and if both necessities applied, essence and another thing would be two complete independent causes of one existence or nonexistence. A necessarily existent thing cannot become necessary **through another** in place of being necessary **through itself**, and similarly with impossible things. A proposed proof says that if the intrinsically necessary were also necessary through another it would vanish when the latter vanished; yet this inference is questionable, since it would follow only if there were no intrinsic necessity as well—the disputed premise.

By contrast, the division into **intrinsically necessary, intrinsically impossible, and intrinsically possible** is **exhaustive and mutually exclusive**. A concept either necessarily exists or it does not; in the second case it either necessarily does not exist or it does not. The three possibilities neither overlap nor leave a fourth case. Strictly this trichotomy analyzes into two disjunctions of contradictories, as does any disjunction of more than two parts. An alleged counterexample such as *the necessarily existent and nonexistent together*, or *that which is neither established nor negated*, is itself a concept whose existence is necessarily **impossible**. We must not confuse contemplating the wording of a conjunction with establishing an instance of it. Nor can intrinsic modality change with time: a necessity that varied with times would not be imposed by the quiddity alone.

**Objection from originated things:** what comes into being is impossible *in eternity*, since beginninglessness contradicts origination, yet becomes possible later. Likewise, the bringing into existence of an effect is possible before it occurs but allegedly becomes impossible after it occurs, since what is already obtained cannot be obtained. **Reply to the first:** if *in eternity* qualifies the **thing** under discussion—*an originated-in-eternity entity*—its existence is impossible at all times. If it qualifies the impossibility, the claim is denied: **the originated thing itself** is possible both eternally and subsequently. *The eternal possibility of an originated thing* must be distinguished from *the possibility that it be eternal*. The former obtains, the latter never does. **Reply to the second:** once the effect exists, its being newly brought to existence is impossible **through the additional condition of its already having been brought about**, not impossible by its own essence; if that extrinsic impediment were absent, it would remain possible as before.

**Third investigation: the material and the modal designation of propositions.** When existence serves as the copula between subject and predicate, the actual modal quality of that relationship—necessary, impossible, or possible—is the **matter** (*mādda*) of the proposition as it stands in reality itself. The mode as conceived or stated is its **modality** or **designation** (*jiha*). These may agree, as in *a human is necessarily an animal*; or the spoken/conceived designation may be broader, narrower, or different from the real matter. A proposition may still be true, as in saying that a human is an animal *by general possibility*, or false, as in calling that same essential relation *specially possible* and so denying its intrinsic necessity. The logicians distinguish designations from matters because syllogisms are constructed and conclusions inferred on the basis of the premises' **recognized modal forms**, not an unexpressed underlying matter of which the reasoner may be ignorant.

There is disagreement whether the **matter** of a predication always concerns its positive connection (so *human is animal* and *human is not animal* concern the same necessary positive tie) or can pertain to either positive or negative connection (so their respective matters would be necessity and impossibility). The former is the more plausible interpretation. The investigators hold that in every proposition existence or nonexistence supplies the copula, and necessary, impossible, or possible supplies its modality, expressed or unexpressed, regardless of whether the predicate itself is a modal term. *The Creator is necessary and existent* means *the Creator exists necessarily and exists as existent*; *the conjunction of contradictories is impossible and nonexistent* is interpreted in a suitable predicative or negative formulation; *the human is possible and existent* means that possibility and existence are predicated of the human. When the predicate **itself** is existence or a modal notion, one must distinguish the occurrence constituting the **predicate** from the existential bond constituting the **copula**, and likewise a modal **predicate** from the modality of the **bond**. Necessity, possibility, and impossibility belong to their subjects necessarily when taken intrinsically; where extrinsic necessity or impossibility is not evident, their attribution to a subject may be merely possible. Whatever is possible **for another** is also possible **in itself**; the reverse is not universal, for something intrinsically possible may be necessary for another as essential concomitants are, impossible for another as some independent essences are relative to particular subjects, or merely possible for another as blackness is for a body.

**Fourth investigation: modality's considerational character.** Necessity, possibility, and impossibility are, for the investigators, **intellectual considerations** rather than independently existing entities. If necessity were an additional existent, it would itself have to be necessary: were its own existence merely possible, it could in itself cease, whereupon what is called necessary would cease to be necessary, contrary to the impossibility of intrinsic reversal. But necessity possessed by necessity would itself demand another necessity, and so on through an actually coexisting ordered infinity, which is impossible. A corresponding proof concerns possibility. Since the same argument appears to apply to existence, permanence, eternity, origination, unity, multiplicity, individuation, being-qualified, implication, and the like, the author of the *Talwīḥāt* formulated a more general rule: when a kind is successively **iterated**, such that each instance of the kind is again qualified by an instance of that same kind, it cannot be an externally accumulated real feature. The general account continues in the following source section.

title: The actuality of modal attributes and the need for a determining reason
en:
... at one time serving as an essential predicate of its bearer in the manner of **univocal predication** (*muwāṭaʾa*), and at another as an accidental attribute of it so that the bearer receives a **derivative** predicate (*ishtiqāq*), must be considerational; otherwise an infinite chain of coexistent real attributes would follow. This is why externally existing properties are not ordinarily qualified with their own concepts: blackness is not **black**, knowledge is not **knowing**, and length is not **long**. **Objection:** why cannot the necessity of necessity be identical with the very quiddity of necessity, rather than an added property inhering in it like whiteness in a body? Then no regress follows, and the same reply would apply to the other cases. **Reply:** if necessity were identical with the necessity predicated of it, that predicate would be applied univocally. Yet to say *necessity is necessary* ordinarily predicates **by derivation**, as *necessary* means *having necessity*. If the claim means merely that *existence exists* because it is existence, *necessity is necessary* because it is necessity, or *possibility is possible* because it is possibility, the proposition becomes trivial and there is no meaningful dispute. In considerational matters, however, the intellect can take numerous descriptions of a single object and stop that multiplication whenever its consideration ceases, without multiplying external realities.

The author of the *Muṭāraḥāt* offers a form of the argument escaping the previous objection. Necessity, possibility, existence, unity, plurality, individuation, and so forth have a common structure: opponents deem them externally existent, whereas we regard them as considerational. Every existent must have unity, individuation, intrinsic necessity or possibility, and eternity or origination. If **possibility** exists, it possesses an **existent unity**, whose existence has an **existent possibility**, which in turn has an existent unity, indefinitely. We obtain an infinite hierarchy of unities belonging to possibilities and possibilities belonging to unities, all genuinely distinct and simultaneously existent. Unity is certainly not the same as possibility. A comparable series would consist of existences belonging to possibilities and possibilities belonging to existences, and a further one of individuations belonging to possibilities and possibilities belonging to individuations.

**Difficulty:** we know decisively that the Creator exists and is necessary, individuated, one, without beginning, and everlasting **outside the intellect**, not merely in our minds. We also know that the human is possible and originated and that humans are many. How then can the qualifying concepts be merely considerational? **Answer:** an externally true predication does not require the predicate to denote an **additional form inhering externally in the subject** as whiteness inheres in a body. To say *the Creator is necessarily existent in reality* means that His reality is such that the intellect, when relating Him to existence, necessarily conceives *necessity*. To say *a human is possible* means that relating the human to existence yields the intelligible *possibility*. Similarly, when a subject is called particular, one, many, eternal, or originated, it stands in a relation to the corresponding concept that must be affirmed, not denied. The absence outside the mind of an independent **principle corresponding to the predicate** does not preclude a proposition's being true **of external reality**, as *Zayd is blind* is true although blindness need not be an added positive entity.

**Further arguments that necessity and possibility are considerational.** It is not disputed that impossibility, as a privation, has no independent external reality, so no extended argument is needed for it. Six arguments concern the other two.

**First:** if necessity and possibility were external properties, neither could be predicated of a nonexistent, since an existing accident cannot inhere in a nonexistent subject. But an impossibility is **necessarily nonexistent**, and a possible thing currently nonexistent remains **possibly existent or nonexistent**. The proof presupposes one and the same concept of necessity or possibility, sometimes associated with existence and sometimes with nonexistence. Yet it may be objected that the failure of **some instances** of a common concept to exist does not prevent other instances of that concept from existing, as with other universals.

**Second:** if necessity were a real existing attribute, the intrinsically necessary being would become possible. One formulation proceeds thus: necessity, as an accident of the Necessary, depends on its subject; whatever needs another is possible; what is possible can in itself cease, even if its existence is made necessary through another. If the subject's necessity can cease, the subject itself can become possible, an impossibility. Another formulation says the Necessary would be necessary **through the attribute of necessity**, which is itself dependent on its subject and thus possible; what has its necessity from the possible is not intrinsically necessary but even more obviously possible, for dependency on a necessary being already makes something possible—how much more dependency on a possible thing. **Replies:** we do not accept that *necessity* is an instrumental ground **by which** the subject comes to be necessary rather than simply the necessary status itself. And a possibility of an attribute's ceasing **through itself** need not entail its actual cessation where its existence is intrinsic to the Necessary's nature, as existence is. The Necessary is what has its existence, necessity, and all such essential descriptions through its own essence, even if a further analysis calls a particular description possible in itself. A proposed reply that the Necessary's necessity **is the very substance**, never an attribute, is weak if *necessity* in the dispute means the necessity or demand of existence: on the supposition that it were a separately real entity, it would have to be conceptually and externally additional.

**Third:** if necessity existed it would, as just argued, be possible through itself and require a cause antecedent to it in **existence and necessity**, since nothing can cause another's existence unless it is itself existent and necessary, intrinsically or through another. If the necessity antecedently required is identical with the necessity explained, it precedes itself; if different, the same reasoning produces an infinite regress. This formulation blocks the easy answer that the Necessary is necessary by its **essence**, not by an added *necessity*.

**Fourth:** if possibility were an existing accident of a possible entity, its subject would precede it in existence, at least in essential priority. But one can correctly say *It was possible, and then existed*, not *It existed, and then became possible*. The answer that possibility qualifies the **quiddity** rather than its actual existence still leaves the disputed possibility as a relation between quiddity and existence, and so posterior to both terms.

**Fifth:** if possibility were real, it would have to inhere either in the **nonexistent possible thing** before that thing came to exist, or in another subject not itself qualified by the relevant possibility. The first places an external accident in a nonexistent; the second attributes it to the wrong subject. **Reply:** *intrinsic attribute* means something demanded by the essence, not something that must already **exist** prior to the existence of its subject.

**Sixth:** possibility is a relation between a possible quiddity and its existence and hence posterior to both; before that relation arose, the quiddity would have to be necessary or impossible, turning possible later. **Objection:** even as an intellectual consideration, possibility follows upon the mind's considering its terms; would not the same change occur? **Reply:** in the absence of a separately existing external relation there is no extramental temporal priority and posteriority. The mind, upon considering quiddity, existence, and their relation, conceives *possibility*, while the quiddity has always been such as to warrant that conception; its status has not changed.

**Arguments of the contrary school.** The previous proofs, strictly construed, establish only that necessity and possibility are not **independent external existents**; they do not establish their being called **positive** or **privative** in the different technical senses. Conversely, the opponents' arguments indicate only that the relevant notions are not mere privations; they do not show them to be externally existing rather than considerational. Consequently the two parties may be arguing past one another. We nonetheless report their customary dialectic.

**First**, concerning necessity alone: if necessity were privative, **nonbeing** would be what confirms and fortifies **being**, since necessity is the confirmation and demand for being. That is impossible, for privation opposes existence. **Reply:** a considerational description is not an absolute nothing; *necessity of existence* has a positive intelligible content capable of characterizing existence as firm or unavoidable.

**Second:** if necessity and possibility were privative, their contradictories *nonnecessity* and *nonpossibility* would also be privative, since each can be truly predicated of an impossible entity, and an externally existent property cannot inhere in a nonexistent. Both contradictories would then be **nonexistent**, allegedly violating the law of excluded middle. **Reply:** a concept's applicability to a nonexistent does not prevent it having other instances that exist, as *nonhuman* applies to an impossible thing and also to a horse. In the present setting *positive* or *existent* does not mean that **every** possible instance of the concept exists. Even if both contradictory concepts had no external existence, that is not what it means for contradictories to be excluded together. Individually considered contradictory **predicates** are excluded when neither can truly be said of any one subject, not merely when neither denotes a separately existing real accident. Contradictory **propositions** are excluded if neither proposition is true in itself. This is analogous to relations such as equal extension, broader, narrower, and incompatible. Applied to concepts, they describe which **things** concepts fit; applied to propositions, they describe which propositions are **true**. *Human is narrower than animal* says that whatever falls under human falls under animal but not conversely; *necessary proposition is narrower than permanent proposition* says that every case in which necessary predication is true is one in which permanent predication is true, but not every permanent predication is necessary.

**Third:** if these notions exist only through intellectual consideration, then the Necessary is necessary and the possible possible only whenever someone thinks of them. But their modalities hold whether or not anyone considers them. **Reply:** a predicate can have no independent reality outside thought and nevertheless be **necessarily and perpetually true of a subject as it actually is**. The conjunction of contradictories is necessarily nonexistent and impossible in reality, although *nonexistence* and *impossibility* are considerational descriptions. In exactly that sense, a necessary thing is, in itself, such that when related by thought to existence it produces the concept *necessity*, and similarly with possible things.

**Fourth:** if the concepts are privative, necessity is absent from the necessary and possibility from the possible, whether or not the intellect considers them; to say *its possibility is nothing* would mean *it has no possibility*. **Reply:** these claims confuse **the description's being nonpositive** with **the description's being truly denied of the subject**. *Its possibility is a privative concept* does not mean *it is not possible*, any more than *its impossibility is a privative notion* makes an impossible thing possible. The intellectually intelligible differentiation of privations suffices to keep the predicates apart. **Objection:** a thing cannot possess a feature unless the feature first has establishment in itself. **Reply:** that principle applies to an externally **inhering accident**, like whiteness in a body, not to every true predication, such as *Zayd is blind*, *the phoenix is nonexistent*, or *contradictories united are impossible*. Some truthful descriptions are affirmative and others negative.

title: Why a possible requires a cause: chance, free choice, origination, and continued existence

... may be directed to one act or its omission without a preponderating motive, do not contradict the principle that a possible occurrence requires a ground. They concern instead the **free agent's determination of one of two equal alternatives**, without a further determinant. We do not concede the impossibility of such a choice, much less its being self-evidently impossible. On our doctrine, the differences among celestial motions, locations, and configurations depend upon this free determination. The philosophers, who teach necessitating causality without free choice, do not accept the resulting particularities as occurring without causes; they attribute them to efficient causes whose detailed workings we may not know. In short, no significant thinker admits that a possible existent simply occurs **without any cause**.

Those who regard the need for a determining reason as **demonstrable rather than immediately obvious** offer two arguments.

**First:** intrinsic possibility entails equality of existence and nonexistence relative to the possible thing's essence; this is what it means for the quiddity to be neutral between them. If one alternative prevailed with no determinant, equality and preponderance would both hold, which is impossible. **Reply:** equality **relative to the quiddity** is incompatible with preponderance **through that quiddity**, not with every preponderance. **Objection:** if the preponderance is not through something else, it must be through the thing itself, since there is no third possibility. **Reply:** this simply restates the disputed claim; the opponent proposes occurrence by chance, neither from the thing itself nor from a further cause.

**Second:** a possible does not exist unless one alternative prevails. That preponderance is something that begins after not being, hence is a positive occurrence requiring a subject. It cannot inhere in the effect, since the effect comes **after** its preponderance; so it must inhere in the agent—there is no third subject. Hence an agent is necessary. **Reply:** preponderance accompanies existence; it is not prior to it, for one cannot conceive preponderance of **existence** while **nonexistence** is what actually occurs. Even if priority is granted, its inherence in the producer is plainly unwarranted. Al-Rāzī actually uses *necessity* (*wujūb*) rather than mere preponderance in the argument. They are connected, since if a preferred alternative can still fail to occur, no preference suffices; what prevails must be necessitated. This necessity precedes the effect, as will be discussed when explaining that a possible existent is encompassed by two necessities, one prior and the other subsequent. The relation of agent to effect is called **necessitation** (*ījāb*) with respect to the agent, **necessity** (*wujūb*) with respect to the effect. Accordingly it is not satisfactory to deny its priority to existence or its description of the producing cause. Indeed, in the *Mabāḥith al-Mashriqiyya* al-Rāzī explains that, even if such necessity were positive, attributing it to the agent would mean that the agent is truly judged **necessarily to produce** that effect. Better therefore to deny that modal preponderance is a **separately existent** feature requiring an extramental bearer: it is an intellectual consideration attached to our conception of a possible thing when judging its occurrence.

**The strongest objections of those who deny the universal need for an efficient cause.** Al-Rāzī reports arguments associated with Democritus and his followers, who attribute the emergence of the heavens to **chance**. The first is a dilemma: if a possible thing needs an agent, its being caused must occur **while the thing exists**, in which case the agent produces what is already produced, an absurd *obtaining of the obtained* (*taḥṣīl al-ḥāṣil*); or **while it does not exist**, in which case existence and nonexistence are combined. Al-Taftāzānī criticizes an account in *al-Mawāqif* which extends the criticism of influence during nonexistence by adding that nonexistence is pure negation and cannot be an effect, and that it is continuous and needs no producer of existence. That misstates a dilemma specifically concerning **production of existence**. Moreover nonexistence is not always continuous; it can itself newly obtain. The attempt to paraphrase the dilemma as combining acts of causing existence and causing nonexistence would make the reference to a cause of **existence** irrelevant in the second case. Al-Rāzī's own formulation says that producing during absence is impossible because there is then no effect, whereas causal action either is identical with its effect or necessarily accompanies it, assuming the effect is posterior to the cause even temporally.

**Answer:** we may choose the first horn, production *in the state of the effect's existence*. If *producing what already exists* means producing what exists **by this very act of production**, there is no absurdity. Similarly, the blackness inhering in a black body is present through the very blackness in question. If it means producing something that existed through **another antecedent existence**, this does not follow. Existence comes about simultaneously with the productive operation. Alternatively we may choose the second horn if the producer is taken to precede the effect **in time**: the effect follows immediately after the instant of causal operation, with no intervening instant. This seems to be the meaning of the reply that the producer's existence entails the effect's existence: upon the agent's existing **under the aspect of producing**, the effect occurs immediately. During the instant of producing the effect is absent, and action on the possible consists in bringing it from nonexistence into existence.

Another objection alleges that if a possible could not occur without a producing cause, examples recognized by experience could never take place: a thirsty person chooses **one of two equal cups of water**, a hungry person eats **one of two equal loaves**, or someone escaping a lion selects **one of two equally open paths**, even when neither option presents a stronger motive. **Answer:** suppose no discriminating reason is presented to the intellect. This still is not a possible event happening without an agent, but a **chooser's actual determination** of one of two equally eligible actions without an additional differentiating consideration. The objection to choice without a motive is a different issue. **Objection:** the choice and determination are themselves possible events that, on your account, have occurred without any cause. **Reply:** they occur through **will**, a faculty whose very office is to choose and specify.

A third objection states that if possible existence needs a cause, **possible nonexistence** should likewise need one, given their essential equality. But nonexistence is sheer negation and cannot be an effect. **Reply:** if nonexistence cannot possibly be an effect, we deny that equal indifference **in quiddity** entails identical needs for a producer; existence can require a cause while absence, incapable of being produced, does not. If nonexistence can be an effect, the allegation that the consequent is false is denied. More precisely, nonexistence is pure negation **in the sense of having no share of externally actual existence**, but it is not so pure as to be unrelated to a possible subject. It is the **nonexistence of a possible existent**; accordingly it is attributed to the continued or newly occurring **absence of the cause of the possible's existence**. The intellect judges that the possible remains in its original nonexistence or enters into subsequent nonexistence because the condition that would give it existence is absent.

**Objection:** absence cannot be a cause, because causality is positive, as the contradictory of noncausality, and requires a positive bearer; furthermore privations are indistinguishable, so none could count as cause and another as effect. **Reply:** the form of a negative expression or its application to some nonexistent instance does not establish that a universal concept is privative in every instance. Neither must the contradictory of a privative always be positive. Nor is the intellectual discrimination of privations impossible. In fact a possible thing's two sides are equal only **relative to the intellect's conception of its quiddity**, so the determining ground for either side in this context can itself be an **intelligible ground**. The absence of the cause and the absence of the possible are distinct intellectual objects; the former may thus be judged explanatory of the latter. This does not imply that a nonentity can cause **external existence**, which would block the proof of a Maker. External production requires a correspondingly external ground.

A fourth objection says that influence must affect either the possible's **quiddity**, its **existence**, or its **being qualified by existence**. Every option was supposedly refuted in the disputes about the nonexistent's thingness and the production of quiddities: quiddity is already what it is, existence is already existence, and the qualified relation is only considerational. **Reply:** production of quiddity means **making it actual**, not giving it its identity as that quiddity; alternatively production of a **particular existence** means making that actuality obtain **for** the quiddity, not making the general nature of existence into existence.

A fifth objection says that if the producer's **being a producer** or the possible's **dependence** were real, each would be a further possible fact needing another producer or dependence, and an infinite regress would ensue. In the realm of externally actual realities, these cannot simply be declared identical with their own causality or dependence. **Reply:** the fact that producerhood and dependence are **considerational** descriptions does not prevent a producer's genuinely producing and an effect's genuinely depending, as already argued. **Objection:** a conception without a corresponding external object must be ignorance, and producerhood and need were genuine descriptions before intellects existed. **Reply:** lack of correspondence constitutes an error only when one judges that the **independent concept or relation** exists externally when it does not. The external thing could have been, before minds arose, such that a mind considering it would form the accurate intelligible *producerhood* or *need*. That dispositional external truth is not a distinct additional relation inhabiting the world.

**Sixth investigation: what accounts for the effect's need of a cause?** The dependence of the possible was established; the philosophers and some later theologians ground it in **possibility**, older theologians in **temporal origination** (*ḥudūth*), others in possibility **together with** origination, and still others in possibility **on condition of** origination. Philosophers argue that whenever intellect considers a thing which intrinsically demands neither existence nor nonexistence, it immediately judges that either state depends on an external cause, whether or not it additionally notices that its existence follows previous absence. They object to grounding the need in origination: origination is a property of existence, namely that existence has been preceded by nonexistence. But existence follows productive influence; influence follows the effect's need; need follows its ground, part, or condition. If origination were the ground of need, or part of that ground, or its condition, it would be **several stages posterior to itself**. Some theologians argue contrariwise that the decisive reason is **origination**, since contemplating a thing beginning after nonexistence immediately brings to mind an explanation for its emergence, even without attending to its intrinsic neutrality. Possibility, they say, is a modal relation of existence to quiddity and therefore posterior to existence, which is posterior to influence and need; it cannot ground need.

**Resolution:** the ground here is a ground **in intellectual judgment**: considering possibility or origination leads the mind to judge dependence. It is not an external sequence in which a separately existing possibility or origination first arises and then produces another separately existing dependence. The alleged chains of extramental priority in the two refutations are therefore fallacious. As **positive arguments**, however, the later thinkers' appeal to possibility is clearer and more worthy of acceptance. **Objection:** possibility and origination persist as descriptions of a possible or originated existent; if either grounds need, need must persist so long as they persist. But causal influence in the preserved being either acts on **existence already obtained**, duplicating a completed occurrence, or creates a **new permanence or other state**, not the continued existent. And if possibility grounds the need, the possible must depend while originally nonexistent, although its beginningless privation is not an independently producible effect. **Reply:** a possible or originated entity's needing a cause means that its **acquisition of existence or nonexistence**, or **continuance in either**, depends upon the obtaining or failure of a condition, so that without that condition the given state would not obtain. This is how the effect continues only while the requisite ground continues. In particular, **persistence of existence** means existence considered in a **second time**. Saying *it existed but did not endure* shows that persistence differs from **existence taken without reference to later time**, not that there are two complete externally separate acts or existential realities.

**Seventh investigation: is one alternative closer to actuality in the possible's own nature?** The majority say that, relative to a possible quiddity itself, its existence and nonexistence stand equally: neither has **intrinsic priority**. One group prefers nonexistence for every possible, whether substance or accident, transient or stable, because absence obtains without the complete realization of the positive causal complex; to make existence obtain, all members of the complete cause must be present, whereas the absence of even one prevents it. **Reply:** just as existence depends on the **presence** of the cause, nonexistence is explained by its **absence**; the failure of a compound condition means only that not all its parts are present. It provides no intrinsic **tendency toward absence** in the subject's own quiddity. Others say nonexistence is prior for transient accidents such as motion, time, sound, and their features, citing their failure to persist. A sounder judgment requires distinguishing two meanings of **priority**. If existence or nonexistence intrinsically prevails in such a way that it occurs without any external condition, the claim is necessarily false: that would make the thing necessary or impossible rather than possible. **Objection:** perhaps its less-favoured side still occurs through a separate determinant. **Reply:** then even occurrence of the favoured side depends on the **absence of that external counter-determinant**. If, instead, one means that an alternative is **closer to actualization** because fewer conditions are requisite ...

... requirements and impediments, or because the requisite causes more often coincide, that is plainly a **priority through something other than the essence**, not intrinsic priority. If, however, one means that a possible thing's essence, as apprehended by intellect, has a **certain inclination toward existence or absence** without that inclination reaching the necessity which would destroy possibility, the impossibility of such an inclination is not evident. The majority offer three arguments to exclude it.

**(1)** If one side is intrinsically prior, the other either cannot occur, and the first is thereby necessary through the essence—making the alleged possible necessary or impossible—or the other can occur. In the latter case its occurrence would either be without a determining cause, giving an intrinsically less-favoured option preponderance without ground, or through a cause that favours it. But then the favoured side's occurrence depends on the **absence** of the cause for its opposite, so it is not preferred through the essence alone. **Reply:** occurrence depending on a condition does not imply that the **priority itself** depends on the condition. The priority under dispute is a mere inclination not reaching occurrence or necessity.

**(2)** Possibility means that the essence makes existence and nonexistence equal, since either can occur only through another. If essence also preferred one side, it would demand both equality and inequality. **Reply:** possibility need mean only that essence does not demand the **occurrence** of one side. It is not inconsistent with a weak inclination that stops short of actual occurrence.

**(3)** If intrinsic priority exists, either some cause can remove it—in which case it is not intrinsic, or can be removed contrary to the principle that what belongs through essence cannot be abolished by another—or no cause can remove it, and then the privileged side would necessarily obtain, so the thing would be necessary or impossible. **Reply:** the impossibility of removing a *weak intrinsic inclination* does not entail that the inclined side must actually occur. A contrary **external cause** can determine the opposite side to occurrence without removing the essence's weak orientation; conversely the roles of the two sides can be reversed. Thus these arguments have not excluded every proposed intermediate notion of intrinsic priority.

**On the assertion “For it is necessary that it reach this point.”** A bare priority or preponderance does not suffice for actual occurrence: the favoured side must become **necessary**, rendering the opposite side impossible through another. Otherwise the same situation could be followed at one time by occurrence and at another by nonoccurrence despite no difference of determining conditions, which is occurrence without a determinant. Thus the possible **must** proceed from its complete cause and then exists. This is **antecedent necessity** (*wujūb sābiq*). Once it exists, its contemporaneous nonexistence is impossible, since contradictories cannot be combined; this is **subsequent necessity** (*wujūb lāḥiq*), called necessity **on condition of the predicate** (*ḍarūra bi-sharṭ al-maḥmūl*).

**Objection:** how could necessity be anterior to existence, either temporally or essentially? Temporal anteriority is clearly false. Essential priority, in the sense of dependence, would mean either that external existence depends on another externally real item called necessity—even though no such independent distinction exists, and if it did, necessity would be an **attribute of existence** and hence posterior—or that the **conception of existence** depends on the conception of necessity, whereas often we conceive existence without first conceiving any necessity. **Reply:** the intended priority is within **the intellect's ordering of explanatory considerations**. In conceiving cause, necessity, and existence, the mind judges that until the possible's cause is realized, the effect is not necessitated; until the effect is necessitated through the complete cause, it does not exist. **Objection:** necessity cannot be described as following the complete cause if it is a necessary part of the cause's sufficiency and existence depends on it; then necessity would be before the complete cause. **Reply:** a part of a complete cause is something whose **extramental** obtaining is necessary to the effect, not a stage of intellectual ordering. Even were it included under the name *cause*, we could predicate consequent necessity of a **partial cause** defined as all requisite conditions other than that necessity itself.

**Objection from free agency:** effects of a voluntary agent need not be necessitated; necessity would cancel choice. **Reply:** where choice is a constituent of the **complete cause**, the effect becomes necessary only after the choice has been made. An effect's following necessarily **upon a choice** does not undo its voluntariness but realizes precisely the chosen act.

**Third approach: eternity and origination** (*qidam* and *ḥudūth*). Strictly, it is **existence** that is eternal or originated; an existent is so denominated through its existence. A nonexistence may also be called eternal if never preceded by existence, or originated if preceded by existence. Both eternity and origination can be considered **intrinsically** or **relatively**. In the first context *eternal* sometimes means **not preceded by anything other than itself**, and *originated* means **preceded by another**; these are called essential (*dhātī*). More narrowly, if the anterior condition is specifically **nonexistence**, *eternal* means **not preceded by nonexistence**, and *originated* means **preceded by nonexistence**, that is, beginning to exist; these are called temporal (*zamānī*), the customary usage among the majority. **Relative** eternity means that more elapsed time of one thing's existence lies in the past relative to another; relative origination means less.

The relation of their extensions follows: everything eternal **essentially** is eternal **temporally**, but not conversely—according to the relevant account, the Necessary's attributes may be unoriginated without being essentially uncaused. Everything temporally eternal is **older relative to something temporally originated**, though a father may be older than his son without being temporally eternal. In the opposite direction, relative origination is narrower than temporal origination, and temporal origination narrower than essential origination. Every thing with less elapsed existence is preceded by nonexistence; not everything preceded by nonexistence is **younger than the arbitrarily selected comparator**. What is preceded by nonexistence is dependent on another; the converse does not necessarily hold.

**No essentially eternal being except the Exalted Creator.** This follows from the proofs of divine unity to be presented later. If a writer calls the divine attributes necessary or eternal **in themselves**, the intended meaning must be **through the Necessary's essence** rather than by their independence of it. Philosophers extend **temporal eternity** to many possible things—separate intellects, celestial spheres, and more. Our theologians ascribe temporal eternity only to the divine attributes, maintaining that everything apart from the divine essence and its attributes originates in time. The Muʿtazila emphasize divine unity by excluding separately eternal existent attributes and confining temporal eternity to God's essence. Yet proponents of **states** (*aḥwāl*) among them attribute to God four eternally established states: **being-knowing, being-powerful, being-living, being-existent**. Abū Hāshim adds a fifth, **divinity**, supposedly distinguishing the essence and grounding the other four. Al-Rāzī, in the *Muḥaṣṣal*, accordingly remarks that despite their strenuous rejection of a plurality of eternals they admit it in meaning, because a plurality of **eternally established** states seems to be just what eternal reality amounts to. A discerning philosopher replies that they distinguish **existence** (*wujūd*) from **establishment** (*thubūt*) and refuse to call the states *existent*. Thus under a definition of the eternal as **what has no beginning of its existence**, the states are not so counted, unless one instead defines eternity through **beginningless establishment**. Al-Rāzī's expression *there is no other meaning to eternity than this* may be intended to block the objection: what theologians call establishment is here used for what we mean by existence, and changing the term would leave the substantial criticism intact. *Al-Mawāqif*'s list of the four states simply as existence, life, knowledge, and power is somewhat imprecise: the technically exact state terms concern **God's being** existent, living, knowing, and powerful.

Hence a product of an agent who truly chooses is **originated and preceded by nonexistence**. Al-Taftāzānī calls this agreement between philosophers and theologians, with denial amounting to mere disputatiousness. A position attributed by *al-Mawāqif* to al-Āmidī—that intentional causation can be prior only in essence, exactly as necessitating causation can, so that an eternal intentional effect is possible—is not presented in his *Abkār* as a settled assertion. This example does not establish that the Necessary **chooses** rather than **necessitates**. Al-Taftāzānī observes that the phrasing guards against the scandal of denying power and choice to the Maker, whereas philosophers' commitment to an **intrinsically necessitating cause** rather than a freely choosing producer is too well known to dismiss by terminological assurances.

The answer is the earlier one. What is impossible is producing something that already existed **independently of this very production**. An eternally dependent effect's continuing existence can be wholly dependent on its eternal cause without any earlier instant at which the effect was absent.

Attributes, though dependent upon the divine essence, are not produced **effects** of it; they are its inseparable concomitants. ... as the agent's **power over it**, and so locate its possibility in the agent, does not succeed. Power is understood through possibility, and its absence where a thing is impossible follows from the latter's impossibility: this effect is within power **because it is possible**, that effect is not **because it is impossible**. Further, power exists only relative to an agent who has power, while a thing's possibility is not intrinsically a relation to any such agent.

**Objection to the philosophical proof of matter:** their eternal possibles—such as primary matter and separate substances—have no antecedent material receptacle. **Reply:** their possibility inheres in them, since an eternal existent has no **preceding period without existence** during which its possibility must be lodged in another subject. **Further objection:** possibility is a description of the **possible thing itself**, and so should inhere in that thing alone. Even if in bodies, forms, and accidents it can be lodged in a receptacle, that can only occur **once the effect exists**, whereas the proof appeals to possibility before the effect's appearance. The philosophers have attempted additional explanations, to be examined below.

**Principal reply:** if the allegedly positive possibility means **intrinsic possibility**, inherent in the quiddity of a possible existent, we deny that it is an externally actual attribute needing a separately existent receptacle; the earlier arguments for that hypothesis were weak. If it means **dispositional or material possibility**, we deny that every newly existent thing requires such preexistent readiness and a material substratum. Something may begin without a prior matter and material conditions preparing its arrival. This does not involve a change of intrinsic modality: what is contrasted with necessity and impossibility is **intrinsic**, not **dispositional**, possibility.

The two possibilities differ in three respects. **First**, intrinsic possibility entails no preference of existence over nonexistence: both are equal relative to the essence. Dispositional possibility inclines toward actuality, being a condition that prepares matter for the producing cause's action. **Second**, disposition admits degrees of proximity and remoteness, as the readiness of an embryo's later stages for developed humanity exceeds that of earlier stages, which in turn exceeds the readiness of semen, vegetable, mineral, elemental matter, and finally primary hylē. Intrinsic possibility does not admit such degrees: the essence *human* is neither more nor less intrinsically possible in the semen than in the embryo. The apparent degree results from associating it with a **receptive condition**, and thus belongs to dispositonal possibility. **Third**, intrinsic possibility is an intellectual consideration without independent external reality. In the latter case, the possibility of one thing being another or having an attribute—whiteness for a body, substantial form for matter, a soul in relation to a body—evidently requires an existing subject of which the predicate could become true. The second attempt interprets the preexistent possibility as **dispositional readiness** and argues that every originated effect has such a readiness. Thus a newly existent effect requires a **newly occurring condition**; that condition requires a further newly occurring condition, and so on. The total set of these originated conditions cannot be a presently coexistent infinite totality, which would be an impossible actual infinite; nor can their entire totality be another newly occurring object requiring an additional member that is both **inside and outside** the totality. title: Graded priority; unity and plurality; the impossibility of two things becoming numerically identical
en:
... in a **shared but graded** sense across the divisions, not equally—priority through causation would be prior or more fundamental, priority by nature stronger where essential constitution is involved, and perceptible order more obvious than merely intellectual order. This proposal rests on reducing all cases to causal, natural, and temporal priority, or only to the first two, and thereby finding an underlying relation of **dependence**. Without such a reduction there is no common meaning of *priority* in all the divisions. **Objection:** they all share the condition that what is prior possesses **something absent from what is posterior**: effective causation in causal priority, constituting or conditioning in natural priority, greater elapsed duration in temporal priority, superior perfection in priority of excellence, and shorter distance from an adopted beginning in order. **Reply:** that is not what *prior* means. If simply possessing something another lacks were priority, every distinct thing would precede every other; if the alleged common concept were *possessing one of these five particular features*, the same trick could make every homonymous word univocal. The word *ʿayn* (eye, source, substance, and so on) could be assigned the purported common meaning *one of the things signified by ʿayn*.

**Fourth approach: unity and multiplicity.** Properly understood, unity and multiplicity are **intellectual considerations** without separately existent forms in external things, by the same arguments developed for necessity and possibility. Their concepts are self-evident even to someone untrained in demonstration, so definitions merely explain terms. Unity may be explained as **indivisibility** and plurality as **divisibility**, or more narrowly unity as incapacity for division into *similar things* and plurality as such division. These formulae fail as exact universal definitions, both in positive applicability and in exclusion, when one considers an aggregate of **heterogeneous** things. Another pair explains unity as *the absence of plurality* and plurality as *an aggregate of unities*. Its justification is that **unity is better known to intellect** as the principle of plurality, whereas **plurality is more immediately apparent to imagination**, which receives many distinguishable appearances and from them abstracts one notion. On that analysis, explaining unity by plurality is an explanation through what is clearer to imagination, while explaining plurality by unity is through what is clearer to intellect; the terms are not treated as equally obscure circular definitions.

**“It is certain.”** Unity is coextensive with existence: whatever has some unity has some existence, and whatever has some existence is one in some respect. But this has misled some into identifying unity **with** existence. A plurality **qua plurality** exists but is not one in that very respect, so the concepts differ. Two proofs also distinguish unity and multiplicity from **quiddity**. **First:** one can conceive the quiddity and existence of something without conceiving its unity or plurality, and even while investigating which belongs to it. Thus one may first prove the Maker exists and subsequently argue for His unity; similarly one may acknowledge the existence and quiddity of the celestial sphere and only later prove its numerical divisions. **Second:** combine the water in several vessels so that it is one water; or distribute one water into several vessels, so that the waters become several. Its unity or multiplicity has changed, while its fundamental quiddity and existence remain. If unity or multiplicity were identical with either, this could not happen.

The dispute whether unity and plurality are **positive** or **privative** is reported both among philosophers and theologians, but the sides shift between two different definitions: *positive* meaning **actually existent**, or meaning **not containing a negation within its concept**. Philosophers argue that unity is part of the one existent, that it contradicts nonunity which can be predicated of the impossible, and that without externally existent unity nothing would genuinely be one. These arguments have the defects already exposed in the discussion of existence and consideration. Al-Rāzī presents a further argument: if unity were privation, it would be absence of plurality; if plurality itself were privative, the absence of privation would be positive, contradicting the thesis. If plurality were positive, it would be an aggregate of **privative units**, and an aggregate of mere privations could not be positive; equivalently, unity as a part of positive plurality must itself be positive. Since unity cannot be privative, it must be positive, and since plurality is made of unities, plurality also positive. **Reply:** even the negation of a privative feature can be privative, as with impossibility and nonimpossibility, so the proof fails.

The theologians argue that if externally existing, unity itself would have to be **one**. Its unities would share a universal unity while differing in distinctive particulars, so every unity would require an additional unity, yielding an infinite regress. To stop when thought stops, or to make the unity of unity simply itself, is to acknowledge the notion's **considerational** character in the relevant sense. They also argue that unity means no more than **absence of divisibility**, and plurality no more than the **composition of units**. The latter does not prove anything independently: it simply assumes the disputed definitions.

**Classification by what bears unity.** Unity can qualify itself, as in *one unity*, *many unities*, or something other than itself. First suppose its subject cannot also be multiplied; if it has no distinct concept other than indivisibility, it is **unity as such**. If it has a further concept, it may be indivisible: when perceptually pointable, it is a **point**; when not perceptually pointable, a **separate immaterial substance**. Or it may be divisible **essentially** as quantity, or **accidentally** as a body bearing quantity. A homogeneous continuous quantity is **one by continuity** (*wāḥid bi-l-ittiṣāl*); a heterogeneous composite is **one by aggregation** (*wāḥid bi-l-ijtimāʿ*). Some also describe as continuous two magnitudes meeting at a **common boundary**, like the sides of an angle, or two bodies whose ends adhere so that one moves together with the other, either naturally as flesh with bone or artificially as links of a chain.

Al-Rāzī says that a homogeneous body **before division** is one by continuity, since its substantial form and matter are one, notwithstanding potential parts meeting at shared boundaries. After it is divided, its separated portions must be capable of reuniting **in actual material subject**, unlike distinct human persons. Such homogeneous parts are thus not only one **in species**, but can once again be one **in material subject**. Separate portions of water agree in species; under the hylomorphic theory, when combined into one mass their formerly distinct underlying matters become one material substratum. On a theory of **indivisible atoms**, by contrast, the atoms can never literally become numerically one substance.

A thing's **unity by aggregation** can rest on **nature**, as with one tree; **art**, as with a constructed house; or **convention**, as with a dirham understood as a prescribed weight composed of six sixth-parts. The six constitute one conventional dirham whether conjoined or separated; five do not, even if contiguous. These distinctions apply to composites; they do not define an absolutely simple unity. In al-Rāzī's formulation they are divisions of the **complete one**, whose available parts are all present, as in a circular line in contrast with a straight line always extendable further. The relevant completion concerns the quantity and possible parts of the entity, not every perfection or attribute. Some later philosophers call the opposite **deficient**, *al-Ṭawāliʿ* calls it **incomplete**, and al-Rāzī sometimes calls it **multiple**.

Now suppose unity's subject **can also be multiple**. One must assign different respects to unity and multiplicity, since the same thing cannot be one and many **in exactly one respect**. The ground of unity may be an **essential constituent** of the many, an **accidental feature** predicated of them, or an external **relation** not itself a constituent or predicate. An essential ground may be (i) the very **specific quiddity**, as Zayd and ʿAmr are one in humanity; (ii) the **genus**, as human and horse are one in animality, answering *What is it?* across species; or (iii) the **differentia**, answering *What is it essentially like?*. The first and third can differ in **intellectual consideration** while referring to the same essence. An accidental ground may be one predicate belonging to many subjects, as whiteness belongs to cotton and snow, or one subject bearing many predicates, as a human is both writing and laughing. As an external common ground, a soul's relation to its body is likened to a king's relation to his city through **governance**. But even here governance can be predicated of each relation, and is an accidental description of soul and king; the supposed further category can therefore collapse into a unity through **common accidental predicate**. In general the ground of agreement must be something predicable either **univocally** or **derivatively**.

**Unity is predicated with gradation** (*tashkīk*), not by mere homonymy and not wholly equally. A numerical individual is more properly one than a species; specific unity more properly one than generic unity; generic unity more properly one than an accidental unity. Among numerical individuals, an utterly indivisible thing is more properly one than something divisible into homogeneous parts, which is more properly one than something divided into heterogeneous components. This does not require literal **intensive strength** or temporal anteriority of unity; those modes of gradation have not been established.

**The concomitants of multiplicity.** Multiplicity likewise admits gradation: a higher number has a greater multiplicity than a lower. **Two is the first number** in the strict definition of discrete quantity; one is the principle of number, not itself a number. It is not acceptable simply to infer from *one is not the first odd number* that *two is not the first even number*. Numbers form distinct species, as their necessary properties differ: even and odd, prime (*aṣamm*, here rendered prime or incommensurable as the context requires), and rationally articulated numerical kinds. Every number is composed of **units**: ten comprises ten ones, not fundamentally five plus five or six plus four, since no one partition is primary over every other, whereas unity is the least constituent, two is compounded from it, and adding one alone changes a number's species. There is **no largest possible number**, since one can add another unit to whatever number is posited. Yet numerical pluralities are **considerational** rather than independent external entities: putting one person in the east and another in the west allows the intellect to judge them *two* without thereby creating a new external attribute joining them. Their supposed constituents, **unities**, are themselves considerational. If two-ness were one actual accident of Zayd and ʿAmr, it would have to inhere in Zayd, or ʿAmr, or both, or their aggregate. It cannot inhere whole in either as that one's two-ness; if in the aggregate, each individual would have only its own **unity**, already established to be considerational.

**Third investigation: numerical identity cannot result from a merger of two already distinct entities.** We exclude trivial senses in which two waters, when poured together, become one **continuous mass**, or water and earth combine to form one **aggregate of clay**, or two things perish and one new substance arises through **generation and corruption** (as in a physical transformation), or a composite changes quality (as black and white become a single resultant blackness). The thesis denies that **one of two distinct entities literally becomes the other numerically**, preserving both as the same one individual. Two arguments are offered.

**First:** whether the two are distinct quiddities, instances of distinct quiddities, or distinct persons of the same quiddity, some intrinsic determination differentiates them. A thing is just what it is through its definite identity; if the distinguishing feature vanishes, **that thing** no longer remains. **Objection:** presented as proof, this assumes the disputed impossibility of an identity merger; presented as clarification, it is not more evident than the original claim. One may be as uncertain whether their differentiation is indestructibly intrinsic as whether numerical merger is possible.

**Second:** after the supposed union either both original entities remain or they do not. If they remain, it appears there are still **two**, not one. If only one remains, the other has **ceased**, which is annihilation plus persistence, not union. If neither remains, both have ceased and a **third** has appeared, which is replacement, not identity. **Objection:** the first horn begs the question: from **both remaining** it follows that they remain two only if they have **not truly united**. The argument is therefore reformulated in the continuation, to avoid taking the intended conclusion as a premise.

Objection: they all share the condition that what is prior possesses something absent from what is posterior: effective causation in causal priority, constituting or conditioning in natural priority, greater elapsed duration in temporal priority, superior perfection in priority of excellence, and shorter distance from an adopted beginning in order. Reply: that is not what prior means. If simply possessing something another lacks were priority, every distinct thing would precede every other; if the alleged common concept were possessing one of these five particular features, the same trick could make every homonymous word univocal. The word ʿayn (eye, source, substance, and so on) could be assigned the purported common meaning one of the things signified by ʿayn.

Fourth approach: unity and multiplicity. Properly understood, unity and multiplicity are intellectual considerations without separately existent forms in external things, by the same arguments developed for necessity and possibility. Their concepts are self-evident even to someone untrained in demonstration, so definitions merely explain terms. Unity may be explained as indivisibility and plurality as divisibility, or more narrowly unity as incapacity for division into similar things and plurality as such division. These formulae fail as exact universal definitions, both in positive applicability and in exclusion, when one considers an aggregate of heterogeneous things. Another pair explains unity as the absence of plurality and plurality as an aggregate of unities. Its justification is that unity is better known to intellect as the principle of plurality, whereas plurality is more immediately apparent to imagination, which receives many distinguishable appearances and from them abstracts one notion. On that analysis, explaining unity by plurality is an explanation through what is clearer to imagination, while explaining plurality by unity is through what is clearer to intellect; the terms are not treated as equally obscure circular definitions.

“It is certain.” Unity is coextensive with existence: whatever has some unity has some existence, and whatever has some existence is one in some respect. But this has misled some into identifying unity with existence. A plurality qua plurality exists but is not one in that very respect, so the concepts differ. Two proofs also distinguish unity and multiplicity from quiddity. First: one can conceive the quiddity and existence of something without conceiving its unity or plurality, and even while investigating which belongs to it. Thus one may first prove the Maker exists and subsequently argue for His unity; similarly one may acknowledge the existence and quiddity of the celestial sphere and only later prove its numerical divisions. Second: combine the water in several vessels so that it is one water; or distribute one water into several vessels, so that the waters become several. Its unity or multiplicity has changed, while its fundamental quiddity and existence remain. If unity or multiplicity were identical with either, this could not happen.

The dispute whether unity and plurality are positive or privative is reported both among philosophers and theologians, but the sides shift between two different definitions: positive meaning actually existent, or meaning not containing a negation within its concept. Philosophers argue that unity is part of the one existent, that it contradicts nonunity which can be predicated of the impossible, and that without externally existent unity nothing would genuinely be one. These arguments have the defects already exposed in the discussion of existence and consideration. Al-Rāzī presents a further argument: if unity were privation, it would be absence of plurality; if plurality itself were privative, the absence of privation would be positive, contradicting the thesis. If plurality were positive, it would be an aggregate of privative units, and an aggregate of mere privations could not be positive; equivalently, unity as a part of positive plurality must itself be positive. Since unity cannot be privative, it must be positive, and since plurality is made of unities, plurality also positive. Reply: even the negation of a privative feature can be privative, as with impossibility and nonimpossibility, so the proof fails.

The theologians argue that if externally existing, unity itself would have to be one. Its unities would share a universal unity while differing in distinctive particulars, so every unity would require an additional unity, yielding an infinite regress. To stop when thought stops, or to make the unity of unity simply itself, is to acknowledge the notion's considerational character in the relevant sense. They also argue that unity means no more than absence of divisibility, and plurality no more than the composition of units. The latter does not prove anything independently: it simply assumes the disputed definitions.

Classification by what bears unity. Unity can qualify itself, as in one unity, many unities, or something other than itself. First suppose its subject cannot also be multiplied; if it has no distinct concept other than indivisibility, it is unity as such. If it has a further concept, it may be indivisible: when perceptually pointable, it is a point; when not perceptually pointable, a separate immaterial substance. Or it may be divisible essentially as quantity, or accidentally as a body bearing quantity. A homogeneous continuous quantity is one by continuity (wāḥid bi-l-ittiṣāl); a heterogeneous composite is one by aggregation (wāḥid bi-l-ijtimāʿ). Some also describe as continuous two magnitudes meeting at a common boundary, like the sides of an angle, or two bodies whose ends adhere so that one moves together with the other, either naturally as flesh with bone or artificially as links of a chain.

Al-Rāzī says that a homogeneous body before division is one by continuity, since its substantial form and matter are one, notwithstanding potential parts meeting at shared boundaries. After it is divided, its separated portions must be capable of reuniting in actual material subject, unlike distinct human persons. Such homogeneous parts are thus not only one in species, but can once again be one in material subject. Separate portions of water agree in species; under the hylomorphic theory, when combined into one mass their formerly distinct underlying matters become one material substratum. On a theory of indivisible atoms, by contrast, the atoms can never literally become numerically one substance.

A thing's unity by aggregation can rest on nature, as with one tree; art, as with a constructed house; or convention, as with a dirham understood as a prescribed weight composed of six sixth-parts. The six constitute one conventional dirham whether conjoined or separated; five do not, even if contiguous. These distinctions apply to composites; they do not define an absolutely simple unity. In al-Rāzī's formulation they are divisions of the complete one, whose available parts are all present, as in a circular line in contrast with a straight line always extendable further. The relevant completion concerns the quantity and possible parts of the entity, not every perfection or attribute. Some later philosophers call the opposite deficient, al-Ṭawāliʿ calls it incomplete, and al-Rāzī sometimes calls it multiple.

Now suppose unity's subject can also be multiple. One must assign different respects to unity and multiplicity, since the same thing cannot be one and many in exactly one respect. The ground of unity may be an essential constituent of the many, an accidental feature predicated of them, or an external relation not itself a constituent or predicate. An essential ground may be (i) the very specific quiddity, as Zayd and ʿAmr are one in humanity; (ii) the genus, as human and horse are one in animality, answering What is it? across species; or (iii) the differentia, answering What is it essentially like?. The first and third can differ in intellectual consideration while referring to the same essence. An accidental ground may be one predicate belonging to many subjects, as whiteness belongs to cotton and snow, or one subject bearing many predicates, as a human is both writing and laughing. As an external common ground, a soul's relation to its body is likened to a king's relation to his city through governance. But even here governance can be predicated of each relation, and is an accidental description of soul and king; the supposed further category can therefore collapse into a unity through common accidental predicate. In general the ground of agreement must be something predicable either univocally or derivatively.

Unity is predicated with gradation (tashkīk), not by mere homonymy and not wholly equally. A numerical individual is more properly one than a species; specific unity more properly one than generic unity; generic unity more properly one than an accidental unity. Among numerical individuals, an utterly indivisible thing is more properly one than something divisible into homogeneous parts, which is more properly one than something divided into heterogeneous components. This does not require literal intensive strength or temporal anteriority of unity; those modes of gradation have not been established.
