Two is the first number in the strict definition of discrete quantity; one is the principle of number, not itself a number. It is not acceptable simply to infer from one is not the first odd number that two is not the first even number. Numbers form distinct species, as their necessary properties differ: even and odd, prime (aṣamm, here rendered prime or incommensurable as the context requires), and rationally articulated numerical kinds. Every number is composed of units: ten comprises ten ones, not fundamentally five plus five or six plus four, since no one partition is primary over every other, whereas unity is the least constituent, two is compounded from it, and adding one alone changes a number's species. There is no largest possible number, since one can add another unit to whatever number is posited. Yet numerical pluralities are considerational rather than independent external entities: putting one person in the east and another in the west allows the intellect to judge them two without thereby creating a new external attribute joining them. Their supposed constituents, unities, are themselves considerational. If two-ness were one actual accident of Zayd and ʿAmr, it would have to inhere in Zayd, or ʿAmr, or both, or their aggregate. It cannot inhere whole in either as that one's two-ness; if in the aggregate, each individual would have only its own unity, already established to be considerational.

Third investigation: numerical identity cannot result from a merger of two already distinct entities. We exclude trivial senses in which two waters, when poured together, become one continuous mass, or water and earth combine to form one aggregate of clay, or two things perish and one new substance arises through generation and corruption (as in a physical transformation), or a composite changes quality (as black and white become a single resultant blackness). The thesis denies that one of two distinct entities literally becomes the other numerically, preserving both as the same one individual. Two arguments are offered.

First: whether the two are distinct quiddities, instances of distinct quiddities, or distinct persons of the same quiddity, some intrinsic determination differentiates them. A thing is just what it is through its definite identity; if the distinguishing feature vanishes, that thing no longer remains. Objection: presented as proof, this assumes the disputed impossibility of an identity merger; presented as clarification, it is not more evident than the original claim. One may be as uncertain whether their differentiation is indestructibly intrinsic as whether numerical merger is possible.

Second: after the supposed union either both original entities remain or they do not. If they remain, it appears there are still two, not one. If only one remains, the other has ceased, which is annihilation plus persistence, not union. If neither remains, both have ceased and a third has appeared, which is replacement, not identity. Objection: the first horn begs the question: from both remaining it follows that they remain two only if they have not truly united. The argument is therefore reformulated in the continuation, to avoid taking the intended conclusion as a premise.

title: Identity versus otherness, inseparability of divine attributes, and likeness among many
en:
... if both original entities exist after uniting, there are still two, not one; otherwise one or both have ceased. **Objection:** the inference once again assumes that two continuing existences cannot have become one existence. An attempted refinement distinguishes whether the allegedly unified things have **two existences**, in which case they remain two, or **one existence**, in which case that existence is either one of the two original existences (the other having perished) or a new one (both originals having perished). **Reply:** the opponent can still say that the two original existences themselves have become **a single existence**, so that neither horn applies as stated. There is ultimately no escape from the denial except by maintaining that it is **immediately evident** that two numerically distinct existences cannot become one. Al-Taftāzānī cautions that calling this evident precisely where it is disputed is not a demonstration, and that impossibility of the two existences' literal union is no more self-evident than the impossibility of the two beings' union in general.

**Fourth investigation: otherness (*ghayriyya*) as a concomitant of multiplicity.** Multiplicity entails otherness only if *otherness* is understood sufficiently generally; the contested converse and the precise definition must be examined. Earlier Sunnī theologians deny that every pair of numerically multiple items are **others** in the special sense. They define two *others* as **existent items that can be separated** (*mumkin infikākihimā*). The qualification **existent** excludes two nonexistent things or an existent and nonexistent: *otherness*, on this definition, is a **positive** characteristic like difference or contrariety, and cannot qualify nothing. Explaining the restriction solely by the nondistinguishability of nonexistents would explain only a pair of nonexistents, not the mixed case.

The condition **separable** excludes part and whole, and a bearer with its attribute, on the assumption of inseparability. It includes two bodies even if hypothetically beginningless, since one can occupy a region where the other does not. It includes a detachable attribute with its subject, whether eternal or originated, since the bearer might exist while this particular attribute is absent. Separability can concern **spatial occupancy** or **existence and nonexistence**; there is no need to stipulate *in one place* or *in absence*, despite a formulation attributed to a shaykh. The account suggests that **separation in one direction** is enough. It also suggests that the attributes which are neither identical with nor other than the essence are the essential **inseparable** properties; according to another account, they are specifically the **eternal attributes**, such as divine knowledge and power, not whiteness and blackness in a body.

Some defend the restriction by the ordinary sentence *There is in the house no one other than Zayd, with his members and attributes*, or *In my hand there are ten and no others besides them, with the ten's units and the coins' properties*. They allege that neither inseparable members nor attributes count as **others**. Al-Taftāzānī regards this as weak: in ordinary speech the speaker merely denies **another person** beyond Zayd, or **another number** beyond ten, not every garment or object in the house; if such linguistic reasoning were literal, Zayd's clothes and all the other furnishings of the house would also not be other than him. Moreover the example makes no distinction between detachable and inseparable attributes.

**Objection:** the created world and its Maker are indisputably two distinct realities, yet cannot be separated since the world cannot exist without the Maker. Al-Āmidī answers that separation **in one direction** suffices: the Creator can exist without the world. **Reply:** that would also include part and whole, and bearer and attribute, since the part may exist without this whole or the subject without this attribute. Others interpret separability as **conceptual**, in both directions, rather than external. Just as the Creator can be conceived without the world, someone may understand that the world exists **without having yet conceived the Creator** and requiring an argument to establish Him. This accords with the statement, attributed to some Muʿtazila, that two others are those of which one may be known while the other is not. The indefinite *one of them* can be used distributively in such formulations. An alleged counterexample—one and the same blackness may be known as a colour but not known as unable to persist, so those two **aspects** would be different things—confuses difference of respects with numerical difference of the underlying reality.

**Further objection:** the world, considered **as an effect or product of the Maker**, cannot be conceived without that Maker, so the proposed concepts are not separable. **Reply:** what matters is separation in the **essences** considered apart from relational characterizations, not in a relative concept whose very meaning includes its correlative. Similarly, a father and son or two siblings are distinguishable **as subjects**, even if *father* and *son* or the two correlated kinship roles cannot be posited one without the other **as relative descriptions**. Earlier theologians accept that when taken merely as **relations**, correlatives are not themselves **separate external existents** and so do not meet the special definition of *others*. That does not deny that the two persons bearing the relative descriptions are different.

An analogous answer handles a substance and an accident, or human capacity (*istiṭāʿa*) and a specified act. In their **identities** they are conceivable as separate, and often externally separable: this subject can lack this accident, and this accident could be present in a different subject. Some deny that accidents endure even across instants. Likewise God could create a particular act immediately without the servant's specific capacity, or the given capacity could, according to some theorists, be directed to the **contrary** act.

Al-Taftāzānī then scrutinizes the form of the *world–Creator* objection as cited in *al-Mawāqif*, where separability is qualified as **in place or in nonexistence**. The Maker, who is neither spatially contained nor subject to nonexistence, cannot be separated from the world under that peculiar formula; al-Āmidī's one-way separation allows the world to be absent while the Maker remains, or to occupy space without the Maker's occupying it, but again includes parts and attributes. Redefining separation as a bare act of **thinking one without thinking the other** does not rescue a formula that still specifies place or nonexistence; and if any nontruthful conception qualifies, even an essential attribute might be thought absent from its essence. Some replies reported in *al-Mawāqif* accordingly do not maintain a single consistent sense of *separation*. A further difficulty is that bearer and **detachable attribute** can truly exist apart, whereas much of the controversy was meant to concern **inseparable** attributes.

The majority instead define *otherness* as the contradictory of **identity** (*huwiyya*, “being the very same”). Given one thing and another, either it is **the very same as** the other or it is **other than** it. This distinction can be drawn in **concept**—human versus *bashar* or rational—or in **external identity**—human and writer, or human and stone—provided the respects are kept clear. The notion that **part and whole** or **an attribute and its subject** can be neither identical nor other is unintelligible when offered as a denial of both contradictories. There is, admittedly, an additional **relational aspect** within *otherness*: *the two things of which neither is the other*. That makes the relational concept more determinate than bare negation, but the qualification is always present in reality and can be implicit in the use of the contradictory predicate. Therefore the majority still say simply that otherness opposes identity and that *others* are two distinct things.

Al-Rāzī excuses the older formulation as an **adopted convention**: they restrict the term *two others* to separable existents as ordinary usage restricts a once broader name for living things to **four-footed animals**. The author of *al-Mawāqif* proposes a different reconciliation grounded in **predication**: predicate and subject are not **identical in concept** but not **other in external identity**, for a true predication requires identity in some respect while intelligible predication requires conceptual distinction. The theory of **mental existence** calls these things **one outside the mind, different within it**; those who do not endorse that account say merely *neither identical nor other*. Al-Taftāzānī rejects both reconciliations. The conventional interpretation fails because defenders of the old position offered supposed **demonstrations**: for example, if *one unit of ten* were **other than the ten**, it would be other than **itself**, since *ten* includes that same unit; and the ten could supposedly exist without the unit. The reasoning is faulty: being other than a **whole** does not entail being other than **each of its parts**. Some nevertheless declared this demonstration certain and treated Jaʿfar ibn Ḥarb of the Muʿtazila, who called the unit other than the ten, as uniquely ignorant. The predicative reconciliation fails because the original discussion includes **nonpredicable parts and attributes**—one of ten, Zayd's hand, knowledge relative to the divine essence, and power relative to that essence—where external identity is not straightforwardly the identity involved in asserting a predicate of its subject.

**Some allow one-way separability.** Another school maintains that for two things **not** to be others, neither may exist without the other; only mutual inseparability suffices. The objection from bearer and attribute is avoided by restricting the paradox to **essential inseparable attributes**, above all divine attributes: neither the Eternal nor His necessary attributes can be absent, whereas whiteness is genuinely other than its body. The part-and-whole case is explained by considering the part **under the relational description of being this part of this whole**: a unit **of the ten** cannot be *of the ten* if the ten no longer exists. But this defence extends to **all correlatives**—father and son, siblings, maker and made—which are then allegedly not others. It would even deny otherness of *otherness* and distinctness of two *contraries*, since both descriptions are themselves relational. One can respond that the issue concerns the **bearers of those relations in themselves**, not the compound conceptual subjects *bearer-plus-relation*. Yet that answer itself exposes the equivocation between external subjects and their relational qualifications.

**The theological motive for the restrictive usage.** Affirming the **eternal divine attributes** appears to imply a plurality of eternally existent realities and at least one eternal entity other than God. Earlier Sunnī theologians sought to avoid the latter consequence by denying that the eternal attributes are **other than** the essence or one another. But Al-Taftāzānī observes that this does not eliminate the **numerical multiplicity of eternals** in the broader sense. The essence and attributes may not be called *others* under a specialized convention, yet they are clearly **many rather than one simple predicate**: the theologians themselves enumerate seven or eight attributes and acknowledge the multiplicity of **whole and parts** even where they exclude the name *others*.

**Likeness (*tamāthul*) as a further concomitant of plurality.** Two items are alike when they share their **essential or constitutive properties** (*ṣifāt nafsiyya*). In this usage, an essential property is an affirmative predicate signifying the very thing itself rather than a further feature over and above it, such as a substance's being a substance, a reality, a thing, or—under one analysis—an existent. It contrasts with a **meaning-dependent property** (*ṣifa maʿnawiyya*) expressing a further positive feature, as a substance's being originated, located, or able to receive accidents. Two implications of likeness are commonly asserted: alike things agree in **what is necessary, possible, and impossible** for them; and **each can stand in the place of the other**. This yields the definitions: alike things are existents sharing all their intrinsic modal qualifications, or existents that can replace each other in the relevant function. But for there to be **two** alike things there must also be a respect in which they differ, otherwise numerical plurality and differentiation would vanish. A view attributed to the shaykh requires equality **in every respect**, and this attracts the objection that it abolishes plurality itself. The next source section continues the argument.

title: Similar accidents, contraries, and the four modes of opposition

... and then, if sameness in every respect is required, two alike items cease to be two, so likeness becomes impossible. Ordinary language permits *Zayd is like ʿAmr* in a respect in which they agree, even if they differ in numerous other respects. In legal discussions, equivalence is often **equivalence in the governing respect**: when wheat is exchanged for wheat *like for like*, equivalence can concern measure, not number of grains, weight, or every sensible quality. **Reply:** the shaykh's requirement may be understood as equality **in precisely that respect which makes the two alike**, so Zayd and ʿAmr, if equally skilled in law such that each could replace the other, are alike **in jurisprudence**, not alike in every property without qualification.

**Whether likeness requires two genuinely “other” things.** Al-Āmidī reports disagreement among our associates about **the eternal attributes**. Some say the attributes are neither alike nor different in kind, because either likeness or qualitative difference between two things presupposes that those things be **other** (*ghayr*), whereas the divine attributes are not **others** under their usage. Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr says the attributes differ through each one's special essential description, setting aside the qualification *otherness*. If he can recognize qualitative difference without requiring them to be **others**, he can a fortiori allow likeness to be discussed without that requirement. Some phrases in *al-Mawāqif* seem to assume that otherness is a necessary precondition of both likeness and difference, leaving the view dependent on one's preferred theory of the attributes.

**“The conjunction of two similars is impossible.”** When two similar things are **accidents**, our theologians deny that both can inhere in **one subject** simultaneously, against the Muʿtazila. If two accidents agree in quiddity and intrinsic essential qualities, there is, they argue, no source of numerical distinctness except their subjects: since their inherence and existence depend on the subject, one subject plus identical essential nature cannot support two essentially indistinguishable occurrences. If nothing distinguishes them, there is no numerical twoness. **Objection:** the accidents can differ by additional incidental determinations depending on external causes, not by subject alone. The same answer meets al-Rāzī's claim in the *Muḥaṣṣal* that every accident's accidental properties are equally applicable to both, so whatever is added to one must also be added to the other, leaving no distinction. It is not enough to object that absence of **our knowledge** of a difference does not establish numerical identity: a sound form of the original argument would show absence of difference **in reality**, not merely ignorance of which two things there are.

Other arguments say: **first**, if two similar cognitions could coexist, someone who already had **discursive knowledge** of a conclusion could undertake another inquiry to **acquire** the very same knowledge, although inquiry presupposes that the knowledge sought is not already possessed. **Second**, one could never be certain that an accidental quality was numerically one, since an indefinite number of identical accidents might inhere in the same subject; yet we often know an accident to be one. **Third**, if two similar accidents could coexist, one could cease and the other remain; since neither is essentially necessary, cessation would require the contrary of the first to supervene, and that contrary would also be contrary to the **remaining** identical accident, so contraries would coexist. **Replies:** the first two infer too much: inquiry might be barred by another condition, such as already knowing the conclusion, and one may know through observation or proof that some logically possible multiplicity is absent. The third is denied by challenging its assumed causal premises.

The Muʿtazila appeal to observable **intensification**: a body first acquires blackness, then more blackness, then still more until blackness is maximal. Our theologians reply that colour-shades differing by **strength and weakness** are actually **different species of colour** united under the graded concept **blackness in general**, and the increasingly dark body acquires a new kind at each moment. Hence the observation does not prove numerically distinct identical blacknesses simultaneously in one subject.

**Contrariety** (*taḍādd*) is another property applying within plurality: two **dependent meanings or accidents** are contraries when, by virtue of their essences, they cannot simultaneously occur **in one subject under one respect**. *Meaning* here contrasts with independent substance: it is something not subsisting by itself. The exclusion of simultaneous conjunction already entails the relevant condition of one time. Restricting the definition to **two accidents** excludes two independent substances, an existent and nonexistence, two nonexistences, and other combinations, which is why the old theologians decline to call legal judgments and mere relational considerations strictly contrary: they are not external accidents. A divine eternal attribute and an originated human attribute, such as divine knowledge and Zayd's knowledge, may appear to fall under the wording; some therefore interpret *unable to occur together* to imply that both could be presented to the **same appropriate subject**. An eternal attribute cannot become an accident of an originated person, nor can an originated accident replace a divine eternal attribute.

The clause **“cannot occur together”** distinguishes contrary blackness and whiteness from blackness and sweetness, which can belong together. The clause **“by their essences”** excludes two propositions of knowledge such as *knowledge that a certain body is now moving* and *knowledge that it is now at rest*, when the stipulated cooccurrence is impossible only because the **external movements and rest** cannot coexist; mental representations of movement and rest can be considered, which is why one can judge their simultaneous occurrence impossible. The clause **“in one respect”** is sometimes explained through relationally opposed descriptions such as great/small or near/far. Their unrestricted concepts may be jointly true of a subject relative to **different comparators**; under one and the same comparator, opposing descriptions cannot jointly hold. Strictly, the extra condition may not be needed once the relevant common subject and mutually exclusive respect have been specified; perhaps the clause is intended to prevent wrongly **excluding** such relative oppositions from the broader analysis.

**Philosophers' treatment.** Everything multiplied is in some respect **other**; two beings may differ in reality, in incidental qualification, or through consideration alone. Two are **similars** if their complete quiddities are the same, as Zayd and ʿAmr; otherwise they are **different** (*mutakhālifān*), whether they share some essential or accidental feature or none. Different things may be **opposed**, as black and white, or not opposed, as black and sweet. Opposites are unlike things that cannot occur simultaneously in a **single appropriate subject, time, and respect**. The difference from the theologians' contrariety is that it excludes **similars** from opposition even if identical accidents could not coexist. The example *blackness and sweetness* explains the subject-condition; the condition of one time is implicit, while one respect matters especially for relative pairs. White in one person and black in another do coexist, so opposition does not mean that two opposite qualities **cannot both exist in the world**.

**Four kinds of opposition.** A standard division proceeds as follows. If both opposed terms are **positive**, they either require one another for their very conception—as **father and son**, which are **correlatives** (*mutadāyifān*)—or not, as **black and white**, which are **contraries** (*mutadāddān*). If one term is **positive** and the other **negative**, the negative may be absence of a feature in a subject naturally suited to possess it, either as individual (lack of beard in a beardless young man), or according to species, near genus, or remote genus: this is **privation and possession** (*ʿadam wa-malaka*). If the negative term is sheer denial without such aptness, as black and **not black**, the opposition is **affirmation and negation** (*ījāb wa-salb*).

Yet no argument establishes that two opposites cannot both be **privative**. The later writers often accept that both a negative and its negation can be privative, as with impossibility/nonimpossibility or blindness/nonblindness. *Nonblindness* can include both **the possession of sight** and **the absence of the subject's natural capacity for sight**; reducing it to just one of these is invalid. A better fourfold division does not assume that one term must be positive: if **one opposite directly negates the other**, the contrast is possession–privation **when the subject's capacity is relevant**, otherwise affirmation–negation. If neither directly negates the other, they are **correlatives** when each concept must be understood through the other, and **contraries** otherwise.

A different proof tries to show that two privations cannot be opposites. **Absolute** privation and a more determinate privation are compatible: the general absence belongs wherever the more specific absence belongs. Two **relative privations**, such as nonblack and nonwhite, can also occur together: a red thing is neither black nor white; indeed it possesses redness, which is not-black and not-white. Further, opposites supposedly must be predicable of one and the same **receptive subject**. Two relative negations cannot, on this theory, have the same subject, because each is anchored in absence of a different positive feature. This requirement is offered to solve two puzzles. **First:** humanity and horseness cannot coexist, yet are not included among the four oppositions if contrariety cannot occur between independent substances. **Second:** blackness and **noncolour** cannot coexist, but they are not strict contradictories (both fail in whiteness), nor simply any of the other three kinds. The proposed answer denies both pairs the required **common receptive subject**.

Al-Taftāzānī raises objections. **First**, nonblack/nonwhite differ fundamentally from **blind/nonblind** or **impossible/nonimpossible**, whose terms directly negate one another; compatibility of two unrelated negations proves nothing about contradictory privations. **Second**, *subject of opposition* need not mean a substance in which the property **inheres**: otherwise all opposing terms would have to be accidents, even though *horse* versus *nonhorse* are plainly contradictories. Ibn Sīnā himself discusses the contrariety of **forms**, taking matter as their receptive subject. **Third**, Ibn Sīnā recognizes subjects at various levels: one **individual** can be just or unjust; the **species** human bears male/female conditions in their own appropriate ways; animal nature may be the common subject for sexual differentiation; *thing* in the broadest sense can be subject to good and evil. **Fourth**, the objection concerns **nonblack and nonwhite**, not *absence belonging to blackness* versus *absence belonging to whiteness*. One cannot treat the bare expression *nonwhite* as though its subject were **whiteness** merely because white is what it negates: by that reasoning white and nonwhite would never share a subject either.

**Oppositions of propositions.** A proposition such as *Every animal is human* contradicts *Some animal is not human*, and is contrary to *No animal is human*. Propositions do not themselves **inhere as accidents in a receptive substance**. Two solutions are proposed. **First:** the same terms are applied to concepts and propositions **by analogy or shared name**. Relations of wider/narrower extension, incompatibility, and equality concern the things **concepts apply to** but the truth-conditions of **propositions**. Thus the contradictory terms of concepts cannot apply to one subject at once, while two contradictory propositions cannot both be **true in reality**. **Second:** take affirmation and negation broadly enough to include both. The **proposition's subject** is the common object to which a predicate is affirmed or denied. Philosophers distinguish **simple affirmation/negation** about terms not intrinsically truth-bearing, as horseness/nonhorseness, from **complex affirmation/negation** capable of truth and falsity, as *Zayd is a horse* and *Zayd is not a horse*. Ibn Sīnā accordingly explains affirmative opposition through **existence of any meaning**, either intrinsically or as a predicate of something else, and negative opposition through the corresponding **nonexistence**, either intrinsically or as a predicate.

**Additional restrictions on contrariety and privation.** The foregoing generic definitions were offered in elementary logic by earlier philosophers. In discussions of natural philosophy some introduce a stricter condition: two contraries must be at the **greatest possible distance or difference** within the common subject, and privation/possession requires another refinement, which is discussed next.

title: Genuine and conventional opposition; truth of contradictories; unity and plurality as correlatives
en:
... as **black and white**, not merely white and yellow; and possession–privation is restricted to absence of a positive capacity in a subject apt **at the relevant time** to possess it. Thus the lack of beard in a fully mature beardless man differs from that of a child not yet of bearded age. The **unrestricted** accounts of contrariety and possession–privation are broader than the **restricted** accounts. They call unrestricted contrariety **commonly recognized** (*mashhūrī*) and the stricter kind **real** (*ḥaqīqī*), since it is the latter they employ in natural philosophy; for possession–privation the labels are reversed, the broad definition being called *real* and the narrow one *commonly recognized*.

This creates a problem for treating the four oppositions as exhaustive. White versus yellow, black versus red, possession of a beard versus juvenile absence, and sight versus its absence in a scorpion or tree are all opposed in some usage, but cannot easily be included in contrariety or possession–privation **on the narrower definitions**. Later philosophers respond that the division uses the **broader** conventional sense of contrariety and the **broader** real sense of possession–privation. Al-Taftāzānī objects on two grounds. **First**, even conventional contraries need not be **two positive properties**: rest relative to motion, darkness relative to light, sickness relative to health, inability to speak relative to speech, femaleness relative to maleness, odd relative to even. Ibn Sīnā and others explicitly admit privative terms among these. Thus commonly recognized contrariety overlaps the other divisions and cannot stand opposite possession–privation and affirmation–negation as an independent species. It is sometimes said to cover only those possession–privation pairs where the subject can pass from absence to possession, like motion and rest, unlike blindness and sight. But even inability to speak or sexual difference or evenness/oddness do not always admit such a transition. Indeed Ibn Sīnā says even and odd reduce under analysis to **affirmation and negation**: an even number is divisible into two equal integer portions, an odd number is not so divisible, so each name combines the common subject *number* with an affirmative or negative condition. **Second**, Ibn Sīnā elsewhere requires **maximal qualitative difference** even for commonly recognized contrariety. If so, white versus red would again be excluded; the classificatory difficulty remains.

**“Among the properties of opposition.”** An objection claims that **correlation** (*taḍāyuf*) is broader than opposition, since one can relate opposites, similars, contraries, and numerous other terms. How then can correlativity be one species of opposition, narrower than opposition and incompatible with the species contrariety? The answer distinguishes **the concept of relation** from **the terms that bear the relation**. To understand *opposite* or *contrary* one must relate the term to another opposite or contrary, so **opposition and contrariety themselves** fall under the broadly relational concept. But this does not mean that the subjects **which are opposed** are all correlatives in the narrower sense, nor that the entities **black and white**, for example, are correlatives rather than contraries. A property can be broader than the concept *contrariety* while the class of entities bearing that property has a different extension from the class of contrary entities.

**“Its predication.”** Opposition is not a **genus** in whose definition every species partakes essentially, for one need not first conceive the universal *opposition* before conceiving its various kinds. This is clearest for correlatives, less clear for contrariety, and disputed in the remaining two kinds. The term is rather applied by **graded analogy** (*tashkīk*). On one account affirmation–negation has the strongest opposition: their incompatibility follows directly **from their essences**, whereas the other oppositions merely imply such denial. A good thing is both **good** (its affirmative essential predicate) and **not evil** (a concomitant negative description). *Not good* directly negates the first, essential condition; *evil* denies the second, derivative condition, and so does not oppose good quite as absolutely. The *Tajrīd* may seem instead to call **contrariety** the strongest of the kinds because it mentions contrariety as the third and says *the third is strongest*. One interpretation argues that contraries display **maximum difference**, hence the most extreme mutual exclusion. The reply is that no difference exceeds a thing's **explicit negation**, whereas contraries entail one another's denial only consequentially. Another interpretation makes *strongest* refer to which **species of opposition most readily admits graded degrees**, since hot/cold, black/white, and motion/rest display such differences more obviously than the other kinds.

**Properties of affirmation and negation.** Their primary seat is **thought and speech**, not an independent set of extramental things. A negation is an intellectual consideration expressed in language, not an added actual entity; otherwise a human would have infinitely many additional positive properties merely by being not a horse, not an ox, not a fox, and not indefinitely many other species. This is the point Ibn Sīnā makes. It does **not** mean that no extramental reality can fall under an affirmed member of a contradictory pair: blackness, opposed to nonblackness, obviously exists in the world. When affirmation and negation are **transposed into contradictory propositions**, exactly one must be true and the other false, even if the putative subject does not exist, because contradic­tories cannot both be true or both false. The other types of opposition need not have that outcome: *the phoenix is blind* and *the phoenix sees*, *the phoenix is black* and *the phoenix is white*, or *the intellect is father* and *the intellect is son* may both be false where the subject is absent or excludes both. **Objection:** if the transposition merely means asserting either opposite of one subject, even the pair *the phoenix is black* and *the phoenix is nonblack* can both be false as **positive affirmative propositions with a negative predicate** (*maʿdūla*) when such affirmatives presuppose an existing subject. **Reply:** in the contradictory case *transposition* means constructing **two opposed propositions**, whereas in the other cases it means predicating the contrary descriptions; the operation has been used in two different senses. Another reply distinguishes a genuinely **affirmative negative-predicate** assertion presupposing a subject from an affirmative **whose predicate denotes pure negation**, functionally equivalent to a negative proposition. In the latter reading *the phoenix is nonblack* means *the phoenix is not black*, and can be true without the phoenix's existing.

Other properties of contraries, including the fact that one contrary need not always replace another in a single subject, are assumed from their definition. **Real contraries**, on the standard philosophical analysis, are the two most distant final species within one genus—blackness and whiteness under colour. This excludes contrary genera such as virtue/vice and good/evil, contrary species from two separate genera such as temperance/profligacy if virtue and vice are distinct genera, and **three or more** contrary kinds, as black, white, and red under colour, or courage, recklessness, and cowardice. A consequence is that **one contrary has only one opposite**: black could not have both white and red as true contraries; courage could not have recklessness and cowardice both as contraries in the strict sense. Philosophers commonly rely on a purported **induction** for this claim. In the broader, commonly recognized use of contrariety, however, they do admit contrasting genera, cross-generic species, and several species of one or more genera.

Al-Taftāzānī questions the account. **First**, the supposed induction is circular: the only grounds given for denying genuine contrariety to virtue and vice, or temperance and profligacy, are that genuine contrariety must be between exactly two species of one genus, precisely the point requiring proof. **Second**, if maximal difference is built into the definition, the requirement of **two** endpoints is conceptually obvious, not discovered by induction: a maximum distance occurs between the extremes, not between an extreme and an intermediate. If maximum difference is *not* required, the principle is plainly false among colour species. **Third**, philosophers speak unrestrictedly of black and white as contrary, even though on their own analysis differing **degrees of blackness** are distinct colour species and differing **degrees of whiteness** likewise. On their theory the actual maximum difference would occur only between **maximally black** and **maximally white**, not between every instance called black and every instance called white. **Fourth**, Ibn Sīnā's admission of several commonly contrary species, such as courage, recklessness, and cowardice, is at odds with his occasional demand for maximal separation even within the broader usage.

**“They say there is no intrinsic opposition between unity and multiplicity.”** Philosophers acknowledge that unity and multiplicity are **correlatively opposed through the relations of constituent cause and constituted effect, or measure and measured**: plurality is made from units; a unit constitutes and measures plurality, and plurality is constituted and measured by units. They deny a **direct intrinsic opposition** between unity and plurality for two reasons.

**First**, opposed attributes supposedly must have **one numerically identical subject**. Yet when a thing becomes multiple, its original unitary identity ceases, and when several become one, their distinct plural identities cease. The intended point is that the **subject of plurality**—the aggregate of several units—does not survive when their distinctness disappears. One must distinguish the plurality itself from the plurality's alleged subject. **Second**, unity **constitutes** plurality, and two direct opposites cannot stand as constituting part and constituted whole. One opposite that negates the other cannot be its constituent; correlatives are simultaneous in concept and, appropriately understood, in existence, whereas a constituent is prior to its effect; and a contrary cannot coexist with what it constitutes, whereas part coexists with whole. **Objection:** if the prohibition simply concerns coexistence in one subject, it would apply to every opposition and needs none of these distinctions. **Reply:** coexistence in a subject need not exclude affirmation–negation if one speaks of a shared **existing bearer** without asserting that the same predicative condition is both true and false.

... **existence**, that is, derivative predication rather than direct essential predication. In the foundations of logic it was noted that for affirmation/negation, conjunction of the contradictories is impossible **by being truly said of one subject**, whereas for other oppositions the alleged impossibility concerns **their actual occurrence together in a subject**. Thus a **white, sweet body** has whiteness and **nonwhiteness** in a qualified sense: sweetness is *nonwhite*, so something describable as nonwhite is externally present in the body, even though the body itself is truly white. There is no contradiction because the contradictory labels have not been affirmed and denied **of exactly the same bearer in exactly the same respect**. What cannot coexist **as external properties** cannot coexist as truly predicated of the same subject; the reverse inference is not generally valid. What is compatible as a true predication is compatible under an appropriate external realization, but mere co-occurrence of underlying things does not establish that the predicates are truly compatible. On this basis, one has not proved that **unity and multiplicity** cannot oppose one another through affirmation and negation. Indeed, definitions of multiplicity by **division**, and unity by **absence of division**, point toward precisely such an opposition.

When the philosophers jointly deny any opposition between unity and multiplicity, they principally mean that **number is constituted by units**, and as so constituted it cannot be absolutely opposed to the units of which it is made. This is correct of the **units that constitute the plurality**. It does not settle the issue of a **new unity which replaces a plurality**, as when water from many vessels is placed in one vessel. The new unity and the earlier plurality may seem contrary, for they successively describe the same water and the one replaces the other. Al-Rāzī denies genuine contrariety because they are not maximally distant and because the original plural units each had **a smaller subject** than the subject of the new common unity. Al-Taftāzānī finds both treatments weak.

**Fifth approach: causality (*ʿilliyya*) and being-caused (*maʿlūliyya*).** These are among the concomitants of existence and quiddity and are **second intelligibles** (*maʿqūlāt thāniyya*), considerational relations without separate external forms. Otherwise the familiar infinite regresses would recur. They are **correlatives**: a cause is a cause only relative to an effect, and an effect an effect only relative to a cause. Cause and effect cannot qualify **one thing in the same respect**, but they may qualify the same intermediary in two respects: an intermediate cause is the effect of a prior cause and cause of a subsequent effect.

**First investigation: definitions of cause and effect.** In the broadest sense a *cause* (*ʿilla*) is **what a thing needs**, and its *effect* (*maʿlūl*) is **what needs it**. Unqualified *cause* generally refers to the **efficient cause**, the source from which the effect proceeds, either independently or in conjunction with other conditions. The items needed by an effect may be **internal to it** or **external to it**. An internal cause may make the effect's necessity **actual**—the **formal cause**—or be a principle whereby that necessity is **potential**—the **material cause**. An external cause may be **that by which the thing is brought about**, the **efficient cause**, or **that for the sake of which it is brought about**, the **final cause**.

The **material and formal** causes are called causes **of quiddity** (*ʿillat al-māhiyya*) because a compound depends on them for what it is, not merely for the existence of that thing, and so its reality cannot be conceived without them or their intelligible analogues such as genus and differentia. The **efficient and final** causes are called causes **of existence** (*ʿillat al-wujūd*) because the thing needs them for obtaining existence but can be conceived in its whatness without explicitly conceiving them.

Six qualifications are necessary. **(1)** The fourfold arrangement is an **organizing division**, not a logical proof that every external cause must be one of precisely two types, *that by which* or *that for the sake of which*; the exhaustiveness there depends upon induction. **(2)** *Material* and *formal* embrace not only primary matter and completed form but appropriate **parts attributed to them**, and the same applies to types of efficient and final cause. Instruments and other conditions can be assigned to these causal kinds according to their functions. Al-Rāzī's classification of **conditions** as parts of **material causation**, since a receptacle becomes receptive only under suitable conditions, is unsound when a given condition is **external to the effect**; he elsewhere himself says a material cause is internal.

**(3)** The distinction between formal necessity **in act** and material necessity **in potency** better follows Ibn Sīnā's usage than the majority's loose language of form as actual **existence** and matter as potential **existence**. Once a form has informed matter, the whole compound is **actually existent with its matter**, so the matter would falsely meet the formal definition and fail the material one. But material cause, as such, makes the compound necessary only **potentially**; its formal principle makes its constitution actually determinate. The majority perhaps mean that form is what makes existence definitely actual, whereas matter is that in relation to which the thing may at least be **potentially** existent; if so, their words require that qualification. **(4)** A **nonfinal component of a complex form** may still contribute only potential rather than actual necessity to the whole: the definition threatens to classify that internal formal constituent as material rather than formal, so both divisions fail to include all and exclude only what they should. Interpreting *potential* so broadly that it embraces actual necessity makes the confusion worse.

**(5)** Restricting intrinsic constituents to material and formal causation presupposes that **genus and differentia** are parts **of the definition** but not parts of the actual species. Al-Rāzī instead bases the division on the consideration that genus differs from matter, and differentia from form, only through the intellect's way of considering them: *animal*, if considered as independent of everything accompanying it and no longer predicable of the whole human, is **matter**; if considered without an excluding condition and predicable of human, it is **genus**. But this works universally only if genus always arises by abstraction from matter, differentia from form, and hence externally simple immaterial beings lack genus and differentia. The investigators explicitly deny that generalization.

**(6)** A requisite condition may be **negative**, such as **absence of an impediment**. If included in the *complete efficient cause*, does this make an existing effect dependent on a **nonexistent cause**? The negative condition is a constituent of the total causal explanation, and the absence of one component prevents the total complex. Yet an absolute nonexistent cannot **produce** an actual existent; if it could, the argument for a Creator would collapse. **Reply:** the power to bring an effect into existence rests on **the existing agent itself**. Other aspects are **conditions of efficacy**, and there is no contradiction in an existent producer's action being conditioned by the absence of something. The intellect can rightly judge that unless a certain impediment is absent the effect will not arise, without imagining the privation to be an externally active maker. This leaves the need for a positive **productive existent** intact. Another response maintains that every supposedly privative condition is a sign of a hidden **positive condition**: wood burns, not because *moisture has vanished* as a causal thing, but because **dryness** is present, which the moisture's disappearance indicates. **Objection:** the **effect's own prior nonexistence** also accompanies its productive cause; would it be a prerequisite of the effect's existence? **Reply:** needing a thing does not entail needing **everything that accompanies the thing**. The antecedent absence of an originated entity is prior **in time**, not an essential constituent of its productive cause. Indeed the notion that existence should depend on its **own nonexistence** as a formal constituent is unintelligible; at most antecedent nonexistence accompanies some genuine condition.

**Complete and incomplete causes.** A **complete cause** (*ʿilla tāmma*) comprises **everything required** for an effect, leaving no other requisite outstanding. This does **not** mean that it always contains a plurality of distinct items. An **incomplete cause** (*nāqiṣa*) is a proper part of the requisite causal account. A complete cause might consist in the **agent alone**, as when a simple cause necessitates a simple effect. Or it might include an agent with a **final end**, as in the action of a voluntary producer whose purpose constitutes a motive; there can also be composite effects requiring matter and form, with or without an additional purpose under the relevant theory. If a complete causal complex contains the effect's very **material and formal parts**, it cannot as a whole be externally anterior to the effect or different from it: its internal constituents are parts of the effect's reality. It is therefore each causal **constituent**, and the complete external efficient complex where appropriate, that can be called anterior; the statement *every complete cause precedes its effect* needs careful qualification.

Each of the four causal kinds can be classified further as **simple/composite**, **universal/particular**, **intrinsic/incidental**, **proximate/remote**, **general/special**, **common/proper**, and **potential/actual**. These are classifications of causal respects, not additions to the four basic kinds.

**Second investigation: a complete cause necessitates its effect.** When the efficient cause exists **with all requisite aspects of operation**, including conditions, instruments, and recipients, the effect must exist. If it could be absent while the sufficient explanatory state was wholly present, its appearing later would be a preference without any determinant, contrary to the established principle. Conversely, when the effect exists, the complete cause with all its operative conditions must exist: need for a complete cause belongs to a possible thing; intrinsic possibility belongs to every possible effect; an existent effect without its complete cause would therefore be an effect whose necessary concomitant was absent.

The complete cause and its effect consequently **accompany each other in existence**. Cause is prior to effect not **temporally**, but **essentially**—by the effect's dependence on it—so one can correctly explain *the cause obtains, therefore the effect obtains*, but not *the effect produces the cause*. **Objection:** this would make it impossible for an originated effect to proceed from an **eternal cause**, since its effect is later. **Reply:** the eternal producer's complete explanatory conditions include a **newly occurring condition accompanying the originated effect**—in our theology, an appropriate determination of **will**; in the philosophers' account, a newly occurring movement or configuration. The producer **considered in itself** precedes the effect temporally; the producer **with every condition required for this particular effect** does not. **Further objection:** production must come **after** the cause exists, and the effect either accompanies production or follows it; so the effect necessarily comes after the cause, even if only immediately after without a measurable interval. **Reply:** it is denied that production follows the **complete cause with all conditions** by a further interval of time; its explanatory posteriority need not be temporal.

**“Therefore the absence of an effect implies the absence of the complete cause.”** This is the **contraposition** of the implication just established: whenever the fully qualified cause obtains, the effect obtains; consequently if the effect does not obtain, the full cause, or one of its requisite conditions, does not obtain. The principle applies **even to nonpersisting events**, such as motion and time, despite the temptation to suppose that their parts vanish despite a wholly unchanged cause simply because their very essences are successive and passing. The more detailed account belongs to the later investigation of motion. **Objection:** two absences are sheer negations; how can one absence cause the other? **Reply:** the relative nonexistence of **this effect** and relative absence of **its cause** are conceptually distinguishable. One may depend on the other in judgment, which is enough for the **cause-and-effect relation in the privative order**; no efficient production by nonbeing is asserted.

It follows that, for the possible's **existence and absence**, there is one relevant efficient source: its existence obtains when the complete explanatory ground obtains; its absence obtains when that ground fails. If absence is **prior** to the effect's first existence, the effect's nonoccurrence depends on the prior absence of its complete cause; if absence is **subsequent** after cessation, the effect's ceasing depends on a new cessation of the operative cause or one of its conditions. **Objection:** sons endure after fathers die, buildings after builders leave, and hot water after fire is removed. **Reply:** the father, builder, and flame in these examples can be **preparatory** causes (*muʿiddāt*), not the complete cause of the effect's **continuing state**. A father prepares appropriate matter for a child's form; his own actions and movements cease when his activity ceases. A builder arranges materials through movements that cease, while the building's **stability** is explained, on the philosophers' theory, by the cohesion brought about by the dryness and physical dispositions of the elements. Analogous explanations apply to enduring heat. On the theological doctrine that God brings about all things by **will**, the continuing effect's direct dependence on Him makes the distinction even clearer.

The producer that accounts for a thing's **first occurrence** may likewise account for **its persistence**, as the sun supplies illumination to a facing object and continuously sustains it. Or the effect's persistence may require some further continuing condition, as ignition requires initial contact of fire while sustained burning requires its continued contact or a succession of sustaining conditions. This gives a qualified meaning to the statement that the cause of **origination** differs from the cause of **persistence**, without treating a continuing effect as wholly uncaused.

**Third investigation: can two independently sufficient causes cause one numerically single effect?** One individual effect cannot be produced by **two independent, fully sufficient causes**, against some Muʿtazilī theorists. But one absolutely simple cause can, according to al-Taftāzānī, cause **several effects**, against philosophers who maintain that a cause one in every respect, with no plurality of conditions, instruments, aspects, or conceptual qualifications, can produce only **one effect**. The first claim rests on two arguments. **(1)** The individual effect would both **need** each of two independent causes, since each is its cause, and **not need** either because the other is sufficient. **(2)** If it depends on both, neither is independently sufficient but only a part of a combined causal explanation; if it depends on one only, the other is not truly an independent cause. The discussion of proposed counterexamples continues in the next passage.

Other aspects are conditions of efficacy, and there is no contradiction in an existent producer's action being conditioned by the absence of something. The intellect can rightly judge that unless a certain impediment is absent the effect will not arise, without imagining the privation to be an externally active maker. This leaves the need for a positive productive existent intact. Another response maintains that every supposedly privative condition is a sign of a hidden positive condition: wood burns, not because moisture has vanished as a causal thing, but because dryness is present, which the moisture's disappearance indicates. Reply: needing a thing does not entail needing everything that accompanies the thing. The antecedent absence of an originated entity is prior in time, not an essential constituent of its productive cause. Indeed the notion that existence should depend on its own nonexistence as a formal constituent is unintelligible; at most antecedent nonexistence accompanies some genuine condition.

Complete and incomplete causes. A complete cause (ʿilla tāmma) comprises everything required for an effect, leaving no other requisite outstanding. This does not mean that it always contains a plurality of distinct items. An incomplete cause (nāqiṣa) is a proper part of the requisite causal account. A complete cause might consist in the agent alone, as when a simple cause necessitates a simple effect. Or it might include an agent with a final end, as in the action of a voluntary producer whose purpose constitutes a motive; there can also be composite effects requiring matter and form, with or without an additional purpose under the relevant theory. If a complete causal complex contains the effect's very material and formal parts, it cannot as a whole be externally anterior to the effect or different from it: its internal constituents are parts of the effect's reality. It is therefore each causal constituent, and the complete external efficient complex where appropriate, that can be called anterior; the statement every complete cause precedes its effect needs careful qualification.

Each of the four causal kinds can be classified further as simple/composite, universal/particular, intrinsic/incidental, proximate/remote, general/special, common/proper, and potential/actual. These are classifications of causal respects, not additions to the four basic kinds.

Second investigation: a complete cause necessitates its effect. When the efficient cause exists with all requisite aspects of operation, including conditions, instruments, and recipients, the effect must exist. If it could be absent while the sufficient explanatory state was wholly present, its appearing later would be a preference without any determinant, contrary to the established principle. Conversely, when the effect exists, the complete cause with all its operative conditions must exist: need for a complete cause belongs to a possible thing; intrinsic possibility belongs to every possible effect; an existent effect without its complete cause would therefore be an effect whose necessary concomitant was absent.

The complete cause and its effect consequently accompany each other in existence. Cause is prior to effect not temporally, but essentially—by the effect's dependence on it—so one can correctly explain the cause obtains, therefore the effect obtains, but not the effect produces the cause. Objection: this would make it impossible for an originated effect to proceed from an eternal cause, since its effect is later. Reply: the eternal producer's complete explanatory conditions include a newly occurring condition accompanying the originated effect—in our theology, an appropriate determination of will; in the philosophers' account, a newly occurring movement or configuration. The principle applies even to nonpersisting events, such as motion and time, despite the temptation to suppose that their parts vanish despite a wholly unchanged cause simply because their very essences are successive and passing. Reply: the relative nonexistence of this effect and relative absence of its cause are conceptually distinguishable. It follows that, for the possible's existence and absence, there is one relevant efficient source: its existence obtains when the complete explanatory ground obtains; its absence obtains when that ground fails. If absence is prior to the effect's first existence, the effect's nonoccurrence depends on the prior absence of its complete cause; if absence is subsequent after cessation, the effect's ceasing depends on a new cessation of the operative cause or one of its conditions. Objection: sons endure after fathers die, buildings after builders leave, and hot water after fire is removed. Reply: the father, builder, and flame in these examples can be preparatory causes (muʿiddāt), not the complete cause of the effect's continuing state. A builder arranges materials through movements that cease, while the building's stability is explained, on the philosophers' theory, by the cohesion brought about by the dryness and physical dispositions of the elements. Analogous explanations apply to enduring heat. On the theological doctrine that God brings about all things by will, the continuing effect's direct dependence on Him makes the distinction even clearer.

The producer that accounts for a thing's first occurrence may likewise account for its persistence, as the sun supplies illumination to a facing object and continuously sustains it. Or the effect's persistence may require some further continuing condition, as ignition requires initial contact of fire while sustained burning requires its continued contact or a succession of sustaining conditions. This gives a qualified meaning to the statement that the cause of origination differs from the cause of persistence, without treating a continuing effect as wholly uncaused.

Third investigation: can two independently sufficient causes cause one numerically single effect? One individual effect cannot be produced by two independent, fully sufficient causes, against some Muʿtazilī theorists. But one absolutely simple cause can, according to al-Taftāzānī, cause several effects, against philosophers who maintain that a cause one in every respect, with no plurality of conditions, instruments, aspects, or conceptual qualifications, can produce only one effect. title: Whether causes can be multiple: two causes for one effect and many effects from one cause
en:
... and if the effect depends on neither of the two supposed independent causes, neither is a cause. The prohibition concerns **one numerically single effect** (*wāḥid bi-l-shakhṣ*). It does not prevent two causes from accounting for **one species of effect** (*wāḥid bi-l-nawʿ*), in the sense that different individual instances of the same kind arise from different causes. Then what depends on one cause is numerically **other** than what depends on the other; no one thing both needs and does not need the same cause. Thus one fire accounts for one instance of heat, another fire for another instance; or one may speak of heat from fire, the sun, and motion as one broadly classified kind, without assuming these distinct temperatures belong to one **lowest biological or physical species**.

Al-Rāzī objects: if the species as such **needs this specified cause**, it cannot come through another; if it has **no need** of that cause by its own essence, it is intrinsically independent of it and cannot later acquire need of it. **Reply:** not intrinsically needing **this particular cause** does not entail having **no need of any cause**. The species can intrinsically need **a cause of some sort**, while the selection of this particular cause arises from the **cause's own determinate efficacy**, not from the generic nature of the effect. Need in general lies on the effect's side; specification of the causal source lies on the agent's side. The kind is, in itself, neither dependent on nor independent of any **particular** source, the determined relation occurring through something additional.

The author of *al-Mawāqif* objects that this would also permit **one individual effect** to need a cause **indeterminately**, being produced by either of two agents while not depending on either individually. The indeterminate conception *one of these two* does not itself prevent **two causes from existing at once**, so why should numerical individuality change the rule? **Reply:** the generic conception *one of the two* does not **require** the two to coexist as independent producers. For a **single individual effect**, its actual occurrence through this cause makes the other unnecessary, and what is unnecessary for the obtaining of this very effect cannot also be its complete cause **in that same occurrence**. For a **species**, each cause produces another individual; neither cause is thereby dispensed with as the source of **its own effect**. Thus a definite individual heat needs the **definite cause that produced it**; *some heat of that species* needs **some member of the eligible class of causes**, and several individual heats can occur through several causes. An individual may consequently have **alternative** possible causes without simultaneously having two **actual independent complete** causes.

One question remains: can **the very same individual effect** be produced **alternatively** by two entirely different causes? If Zayd moves a given stone through a certain trajectory at a certain time, would a movement along exactly that trajectory at exactly that time, caused by ʿAmr instead, be **numerically the same movement**? The answer turns on whether **numerical identity of the producer** enters into **numerical individuation of the effect**. This differs from the later question whether a **temporally extended movement** can preserve its identity when one agent causes an earlier part and another a later part. The issue is the counterfactual replacement of all the moving agents, not their dividing the parts of one motion.

**Argument of those who allow two independent causes of one individual effect.** Imagine a single indivisible atom attached both to Zayd's hand and ʿAmr's, with Zayd pushing and ʿAmr pulling **at the same instant and with equal speed and strength**. Its motion is one numerical event, since two identical motions cannot coexist in the same simple subject. Yet allegedly the motion independently proceeds from both agents, since nothing makes one producer preferred to the other. **Reply:** we deny their **independent** causality. Both may be **partial causes of one effect**; a compound cause need not yield a numerically composite effect whose parts distribute among the cause's constituents. Or the true immediate source of the movement is the Necessary, according to the theological doctrine the author favours.

**The opposite problem: can one absolutely simple agent produce several effects?** We affirm this against the philosophers' dictum that an absolutely one cause—without diverse conditions, instruments, aspects, or considerations—can immediately produce **one thing only**. Two reasons support our position. **First**, no intrinsic or extrinsic contradiction is evident in multiple effects arising from one simple agent; the claimant of impossibility owes a demonstration. This is an **argument of plausibility** rather than demonstrative proof. **Second**, the later proof that all possible things depend on the **one Necessary Existent** supplies a substantive theological ground for universal production. The philosophical arguments must nevertheless be considered.

**Philosophers' first proof.** If one simple cause produces two effects, its **being the source of this one** and **being the source of that one** are distinct concepts. They cannot both be simply identical with the source; one or both must be an **intrinsic constituent**, destroying simplicity, or an **external concomitant** caused by that simple source, in which case the source has a further sourcehood for the concomitant, and a regress of causal qualifications arises within a supposedly bounded hierarchy.

Al-Taftāzānī records six objections. **(1)** *Being a source of* is a **considerational relation**, not an independently existing part of the agent or an accident needing a further efficient cause. **(2)** The two sourcehoods are distinct **in conception**, not necessarily as externally distinct realities. **(3)** If each sourcehood had an independent external identity, even the production of **one** effect would destroy the agent's absolute simplicity through the further externally real sourcehood. **(4)** Were sourcehood external to its agent, it would not follow without additional argument that **its own efficient cause** must be the same agent; it might derive from another source. The exception would be where the original source is the **Necessary** from whom all others depend, but that narrows the universal proposition. **(5)** If the Necessary produces even one effect and externally distinct sourcehood must itself be produced by the Necessary, then this additional produced sourcehood generates another, indefinitely, so the philosophers' reasoning implies the infinite regress they wished to avoid. **(6)** The proof would forbid a simple thing from **producing any effect at all**, and even from bearing multiple true **negations**, **attributes**, or **receptive capacities**, since the distinct concepts *not-stone*, *not-tree*, *able-to-stand*, *able-to-sit*, *capable-of-motion*, and *capable-of-blackness* would, by the same argument, have to become intrinsic components or external accidents requiring new sources. That conclusion is absurd.

Philosophers attempt a general answer. Negations, attributive connections, and capacities are merely **intellectual relations** with no differentiated external realities. In any event, they are not attributed to a bare simple source **qua simple**, but presuppose distinctions between **subject and denied predicate**, **bearer and property**, or **receptacle and receivable state**. Production, they say, differs: besides the merely relative description of the link between cause and effect there is a **genuine positive feature** making the cause such that its effect **necessarily proceeds**. The mere hypothesis of a **single agent** suffices to ground this feature; otherwise all effects could not be traced to a single first principle. Since a feature of being-such-as-to-produce is itself seemingly relational and considerational, they recast it as a **specific positive disposition or qualification** corresponding to a particular effect. When we successively perform distinct movements, we acquire some different causal specification for each—at minimum a different **act of will**. Likewise all finite causes that produce different effects must possess a relevant specification for each. If the cause is productive **through its very essence**, that specification is its essence; if productive through another determination, it is an additional state. Producing several effects must therefore entail several causal respects, whereas producing **one** entails only one relevant respect and need add nothing to the essence.

Al-Taftāzānī replies that most of these alleged premises are **unsupported assumptions**, scarcely supported by plausible considerations, much less by demonstrations. Another form of the proof is offered as a supposedly clearer restatement: if two effects derive from a truly one agent, the concept *cause of A* differs from *cause of B*; a thing qualified by one distinct concept differs from a thing qualified by the other; hence the source cannot be one absolutely simple thing, but must be two, or one bearer of two attributes. By contraposition, absolute unity of cause implies unity of effect. Yet this restatement has **little demonstrative value**, and if taken literally it destroys the many metaphysical arguments built on the prohibition of multiple emanations from a simple principle. A simple source may cause many effects while the intellect conceives **different sourcehood relations** toward each; their conceptual difference does not compromise the source's external unity. Otherwise the cause's own sourcehood toward its **one** effect would differ in concept from its essence and would already destroy its simplicity.

**Second philosophical proof.** If an absolutely one cause produces **A** and also **B**, it both produces **A** and produces **not-A** (since B is not A); hence it combines contradictories. Only multiple causal respects allegedly avoid the conjunction. Al-Taftāzānī declares the fallacy obvious: the contradictory of *produces A* is **does not produce A**, not **produces something other than A**. Producing A and producing B, where B is not A, is not a contradiction. Al-Rāzī expresses amazement that someone might spend a lifetime studying logic to avoid error yet abandon it at a central metaphysical question and fall into a mistake obvious to children. A further reconstruction says that **nonproduction of A** can be predicated of **production of not-A**, so when one source produces A and not-A it has both production and nonproduction of A. But the relevant prohibition is that two contradictories be **truly predicated of the same subject** univocally; it does not prohibit different intelligible relations or features being present and described derivatively. A white, sweet thing contains whiteness and an item called *nonwhite* in the sense that sweetness is not whiteness, yet the body is not both white and not white as a contradictory pair of affirmations. So also the agent's causing A and some non-A does not entail that it both caused and did not cause A. A version in *al-Ṣaḥāʾif* also confuses *does not produce A* with *produces something that is not A*.

**Third philosophical proof.** If a single source could produce distinct effects, the distinctness of effects would not establish distinctness of their causes. Yet human reason routinely infers a difference in sources from differences in effects: fire heats a neighbouring thing, water cools it, so the two sources differ in their natures. **Reply:** the reasoning depends not on the general proposition that every different effect requires a different source, but on the proposition that the **presence of a complete productive nature necessitates its characteristic effect**. When water produces no heating characteristic of fire, it lacks that particular full causal nature. Thus the observed difference in effects is evidence of a difference in those causes' operative features, not a proof that one perfectly simple agent can never produce two effects. The original discussion continues to answer this and other arguments in the following source section.
